taskTitle: Let's isolate the Staging and Production Environments !!
content:
Summary

Your organization has recently decided to adopt serverless architectures to build its next generation of service APIs. The development teams have been using AWS API Gateway and AWS Lambda to build powerful APIs to their customers. However, developers have been using a single environment to build and test the APIs and now need your help to build fully isolated environments for testing (staging) and production purposes. They know it is important to separate these environments so that they can continue to improve the APIs without affecting customers using a stable version of the APIs in production.

You were tasked to create a blue/green deployment model that could serve as basis for deploying the various service APIs currently being developed within your organization. The blue/green model must enforce the full isolation of the "staging" (green) and the "production" (blue) environments.

You have no time to waste! So, you started by creating a very simple API called Greeting API that will help you build and test your model. Then, you created two API Gateway stages (staging and prod), a Lambda function (GreetingLambda) that implements the API logic, and two Lambda aliases (staging and prod). Your plan is to have the "staging" API endpoint resolve to the "staging" Lambda alias and the "prod" API stage resolve to the "prod" Lambda alias. This way new changes made to the Lambda code can be deployed to the "staging" alias first and be visible only from the "staging" API endpoint. When you're ready to push the changes to production you can simply update the "prod" Lambda alias to point to the same Lambda version referenced by the "staging" alias. Things look great and you're confident that you have all the pieces in place (ie, two API stages and two Lambda aliases).

But, wait... When you hit the production and staging API endpoints from your web browser you always get the same results back even if new changes were deployed only to the staging environment. Hmmm, that's intriguing... You now have to dive deep and figure out what configuration is missing to fully isolate the production and staging environments.

Important Parameters

Take note of the following stack outputs (under Output Properties):

  • APIStagingStageGreetingURL: URL of the staging (Green) API environment
  • APIProdStageGreetingURL: URL of the production (Blue) API environment
  • CheckChallengeAnswerURL: URL that will give the answer to this challenge once you solve it

Solving this Challenge

First things first... So, let's start troubleshooting the problem. Your first goal will be to make a small change to the Lambda code and deploy it as a new version into the "staging" environment only. Follow the steps below.

Step #1: Make a small change to the Lambda function code

Open the AWS Lambda Console and click on your Lambda function: GreetingLambda. You should now see the Lambda editor. Use the editor to replace the greeting string from "Hello" to "Hi", in the source code. Hit "Deploy", wait for the deployment to complete then hit Test" to test your Lambda changes. The console might ask you to create a test event. If so, use the "Hello World" test event as a reference. Enter an event name (eg, "GreetingTestEvent") and in the event template type this JSON input: {"name": "awsstudent"} (delete the default event template: {"key3": "value3", ...}). Hit "Create" to create the test event. Click on "Test" to run the Lambda function. Now, expand the "Execution result" panel by clicking on "details" to see the output logs of the Lambda execution. Did you notice that now the function greets you with {"greeting": "Hi, awsstudent!"}?

Now that you have made a change to the Lambda code you will deploy it into the "staging" environment. This is accomplished by publishing a new version of the Lambda code and updating the "staging" alias to point to that new version. Follow step #2 below.

Step #2: Publish a new version of the Lambda function code and deploy it to the "staging" environment.

Still on the Lambda Console, click on "Versions" and then "Publish new version". Use a simple version description like "version 2". Note that you are only able to publish a new version of the Lambda function because you have changed the Lambda code. If you go back to the Lambda function main screen and click on "Versions" you should be able to see multiple versions of your Lambda function now. You will also notice that the two Lambda aliases (staging and prod) refer to version 1. Let's update the staging alias to point to version 2, the version that contains the code changes you made in the previous step. Back in the Lambda function main screen, click on "Aliases". Select the staging alias by clicking on the corresponding radio button then hit the "Edit" button. Update the Lambda version in the staging alias to version 2 and hit "Save". Now click on the alias name (should be a clickable link) and hit "Test" to run the Lambda function. Expand the Lambda execution logs panel again by hitting "Execution results", at the top of the page, and then "details". Did you notice that now the staging alias returns {"greeting": "Hi, awsstudent!"}? Now do the same procedure but selecting the prod alias and notice that the output produced is different: {"greeting": "Hello, awsstudent!"}, as expected! That's great. This means that your changes only affected the staging environment.

So, the Lambda aliases are working just fine and you are able to deploy changes to the "staging" alias without affecting the "prod" alias. Your next step will be to troubleshoot the API Gateway configuration.

Step #3: Troubleshoot the API Gateway configuration.

Open your web browser, hit the staging and production API endpoints again (find the URLs from Output Properties APIStagingStageGreetingURL and APIProdStageGreetingURL). What do you see? Both endpoints return {"greeting": "Hi, awsstudent!"}? But, why? Why do both endpoints now return "Hi" if you only updated the "staging" Lambda alias in steps #1 and #2?

Since you have tested your Lambda aliases and they are working just fine the issue must be an API Gateway misconfiguration. Congrats, you have narrow down the issue. Most of your troubleshooting work will now take place in the API Gateway Console!

Now, to the real deal! Your tasks in this challenge are:

  • To troubleshoot the API misconfiguration and figure out why both API endpoints ("staging" and "prod") return the same results despite the fact that you only updated the staging Lambda alias
  • To fix the issue so that these API endpoints return the expected results (eg, {"greeting": "Hi, awsstudent!"} for staging (reflecting your changes to the Lambda code) and {"greeting": "Hello, awsstudent!"} for prod)

How do I know that I've solved this challenge?

Open a web browser and visit the URL indicated in the Output Property CheckChallengeAnswerURL. The answer to this challenge will be revealed to you once you have solved the challenge.

Good luck!

taskTitle: Call Amazon Bedrock from AWS Lambda
content:
## Background:
AnyTaxCity was able to find a sample chatbot application online which they set up in their AWS account. 
This chatbot uses a simple html front-end in Amazon S3, which is put behind a Amazon CloudFront Distribution. 

For the backend  of this application the sample chatbot uses an Amazon API gateway which sends the requests to an AWS Lambda function. This AWS Lambda function takes the user input and sends the request to the *Amazon Nova Lite* Model in Amazon Bedrock and responds with the generated output.

## Your Task

This sample chatbot uses the knowledge of the pretrained model to respond to questions. Adjust the Lambda function (*GenAI-chatbot-backend-LambdaFunction*) to use [retrieval augmented generation with Amazon Bedrock](https://boto3.amazonaws.com/v1/documentation/api/1.35.8/reference/services/bedrock-agent-runtime/client/retrieve_and_generate.html). Also, make sure you enable model access to the *Nova Lite* model in the account.

You can test this sample application using the Amazon Cloudfront distribution link in the output parameters of the JAM platform.

## Inventory
The following resources have been pre-created for this challenge:
- AWS Lambda function to process requests to the chatbot.
- Amazon S3 bucket with front-end code.
- Amazon CloudFront distribution to server the front-end. 
- Amazon API Gateway to send the API's from the front-end to.
- Knowledge base for Amazon Bedrock, which was created in the previous task.



## Services you should use
- AWS Lambda
- Amazon Bedrock (SDK)

## Validation
Once you have successfully set up the Knowledge Base for Amazon Bedrock and changed the AWS Lambda code to call the *RetrieveAndGenerate* API, you can test your chatbot via the Amazon CloudFront URL provided in the output parameters.

To validate the code, ask the chatbot the following question: "What is the flat income tax rate of AnyTaxCity?". The numeric answer to this question is the answer you need to put into the textbox. 


### Factors that must be true for the task to be successful: 
- After you created the Knowledge base, you will need to 'sync' the data source you set up to ensure the Knowledge Base for Amazon Bedrock gets populated. Make sure you enabled the correct Amazon Bedrock models to do this.
- Change the AWS Lambda function (*GenAI-chatbot-backend-LambdaFunction*) to perform RAG using Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock

## Important Information

You are using a training account with limited access to Amazon Bedrock. Due to the service quotas set for Requests per Minute (RPM), Tokens per Minute (TPM) and Tokens per Day (TPD) , you may encounter throttling issues. To mitigate these issues:

    Execute code blocks one at a time. If you receive an error, wait a few seconds before retrying.
    Avoid running multiple operations concurrently.
    If throttling persists, wait 2 minutes before running any code that interacts with Bedrock.
    If the problem continues after waiting, you may need to end the lab and start again.

We understand this is not ideal and are working hard to implement a permanent solution. Following these steps will help ensure a smoother experience as you explore Amazon Bedrock’s capabilities. In the interim, please provide the details of any problems you encounter using the https://support.aws.amazon.com/#/contacts/aws-training.

taskTitle: Slap a Façade on that Monolith!
content:
### Background

In order to get the New Policies Application out of the data center, you have done a "lift-and-shift' of the Monolithic Application on to EC2 in AWS. A refactor environment is deployed for you using Refactor Spaces, A Refactor Spaces environment provides the infrastructure, multi-account networking, and routing needed to incrementally modernize applications. Refactor Spaces environments include an application proxy that models the Strangler Fig pattern to let you transparently add new services to an external HTTPS endpoint and incrementally route traffic to the new services. Refactor Spaces optionally bridges networking across AWS accounts to allow legacy and new services to communicate while maintaining the independence of separate AWS accounts.

##### Your Task

Your first task is to create a new Default Service in your Refactor Spaces environment that represents the existing EC2 Monolith Application. Include the route as default to the monolith EC2 when you create the service. Ensure you activate the route. Use the Monolith Endpoint from the OUTPUTS section, and do not include the trailing forward slash ("/" at the end).


### Inventory
- Refactor Spaces Environment and Application (refer to Output Properties)
- Monolith URL (refer to Output Properties)

- EC2

That new policy information is used for various functions, such as customer service, accounting, and a customer pet portal capability.

##### **Your Task**
In order to send the same New Customer Policy Request data to multiple microservices, you need to create a new Simple Notification Service (SNS) Topic in AWS. The downstream microservices can then be added as subscribers to the Topic.

Get Started by creating a New SNS Topic called NewPolicyRequests in the AWS Console. 
- Select "Standard" Topic type, enter the Name as "NewPolicyRequests", and leave all other options as defaulted values. 
- Make note of the ARN of the Topic as you will need to add it to the NewPolicyRequest Lambda function.

Once you have created the NewPolicyRequests Topic, you will need to update the NewPolicyRequest Lambda Function to send messages to the Queue. 
- Since we aren't teaching you Python in this task, we have provided you with the code in the lambda function, and commented it out. 
- You only need to remove the hash (#) in order to re-enable the code.

1. Go to the Lambda Function console in AWS, open the NewPolicyRequest Function and review the code; "Un-comment" the code that creates the SNS Boto3 client by deleting the hash(#)and space before the line. You are looking for this:

```# sns = boto3.client('sns', config=config)```

2. Then, scroll down to the bottom of the code and "Un-comment" the entire block that sends the event to the SNS Topic. Be sure to REPLACE "yourTopicArnHere" with the ARN of the new Topic you created!!! You are looking for this:

```
 response = sns.publish(

```

taskTitle: Limit the number of messages, so the Large Account Notification Team doesn't get mad at you.
content:
### Background
You have created the microservice for the New Customer Pet Policy Application in AWS (the NewPolicyRequest Lambda), and you have also created the facade with a default route to the monolith (RefactorSpaces Service). Your microservice is going to use the Fan Out architecture pattern to deliver data to downstream microservices. 

One of those services is the "Large Account" service. This microservice should only receive notifications when the new customer policy request has **more than 2 pets** listed on the policy. 

This is an easy thing to do, because if there is a "pettype2" listed, we know there are at least two pets!
##### **Your Task**
To get started, go to the SNS Console and create a new subscription for the existing "LargeAccountNotification" Lambda.

1. Toggle the "Subscription filter policy" button to show the subscription filter policy input section.

2. You must select "Message Attributes" type of filter.
3. Copy and paste this snippet into the json section, which will filter out any messages that do not have a "pettype2":
```
{
    "pettype2": [{"exists": true}]
}
```

Save the subscription to complete.

### Inventory
- LargeAccountNotification Lambda

### Services you should use
- Lambda ARN
- SNS Topic, SNS Subscription


### Task Validation
This task will complete automatically. You can optionally trigger the check by the "Check my progress" button

taskTitle: Application can't access its S3 Bucket
content:
## Background
You participated an application modernization project.

As an infrastracture architect, you're requested by the application team to provide a S3 bucket and an IAM role for their Lambda function to use based on their CRUD design.
You've written a CloudFormation template and deployed it onto the test account.

However, a few hours later, you received a complaint from them - *hey, our Lambda function can't read/write any object from/to the bucket!*

According to them, the Lambda function resides within the same account.

## Your Task
Look into resources you've created to find out what was wrong. What you've created are a S3 bucket and an IAM role - looks like either is a culprit.
Once found, edit the suspicious part directly to isolate the problem, so that you'll be able to modify CloudFormation template later on.

**Note:**
See *Output Property* section of the Jam challenge to find out name of the S3 bucket and the IAM role on which you have to work.

## Getting Started
Open Management Console to take a look.

## Inventory: Resources you need to use in this task
- S3 Bucket

taskTitle: Zero-Downtime Zone:  Agent Navigates Complex Deployments
content:
You have successfully progressed through your AI transformation journey by resolving pipeline issues and establishing an intelligent assistant using Amazon Bedrock Agents. Now, you are entering the final phase: implementing automated Lambda code upgrades and deployments using your AI infrastructure.

In this task, you will leverage the UpgradeRollOut Agent (Amazon Bedrock Agent), connected to TechCore's rollout upgrade knowledge base, to orchestrate a complete Lambda upgrade and deployment process.


## Your Tasks
Your Bedrock agent understands the deployment strategies from the knowledge base, but now it needs to **take action** - actually execute deployment commands, and make real-time decisions during the upgrade process. 

Now the fixed code for particular lambda function is uploaded and kept in S3 bucket. You need to upgrade the lambda function with the new code which will create a new version of lambda. And you need to roll out the deployment to new version using specific deployment strategy which is mentioned in knowledge base of the agent. 

Before querying the agent please make sure you are using the version of the agent which was attached to the Knowledge Base in Task2. And also do check that you have provided the same description while attaching knowledge base to the agent as mentioned in Task2. 

The entire upgrade and rollout follows this **single flow**:  

---

### Step 1 – Identify & Update Lambda Code
- Query the ```Knowledge Base``` using agent:  
  - Can you help me find lambda functions which needs to be fixed and rolled out.
  - Can you share with me all the configurations for upgrading and deploying ```Name of the Lambda function``` please provided in proper format.

- Replace the ```placeholder```  in the S3 bucket location with the region where your challenge runs.  
- Use the agent to ```update the Lambda code```.  
- ```code version``` found in Knowledge base (⚠️ this is **not** the AWS Lambda version)
- Note Down the new ```published Lambda version``` created after the update.  

---

### Step 2 – Set Up CodeDeploy using Agent
- Ask agent to provide all the configuration for specific lambda for rolling out its new version using codedeploy.
- Create a ```CodeDeploy application``` (name must match the name present in knowledge base).  
- Create a ```Codedeploy Deployment Group``` linked to the Lambda alias:  
  - Use the ```ServiceRoleArn``` from the JAM console output properties.  
- Prepare an ```AppSpec file``` that maps:  
  - The Lambda function name  
  - Alias (still pointing to old version)  
  - New version of Lambda (which you got in Step 1) to roll out.
- Create ```CodeDeploy Deployment```. 
- After this you can monitor the deployment in Codedeploy service. 

---

```FLOW``` of RollingOut upgrade using UpgradeRollOutAgent will be:

```UpdateLambda Code``` -> ```CreateDeploymentApplication``` -> ```CreateDeploymentGroup``` -> ```CreateAppsec``` -> ```CreateDeployment```

    You can start by asking "Let's proceed to first step, and which parameters are needed for that".
---
Checkout the  ```Output Properties``` of JAM console to get specific resource ID's which are used are in tasks (ServiceRoleArn, Knowledgbase).

Once all 5 steps are completed proceed to AWS CodeDeploy service in console and under <span style="color:orange">Deployment</span> you can monitor the CodeDeploy rolling out the Lambda from older version to new version.

**NOTES**: 
- ```Names``` when deploying the infrastructure of Codedeploy should match the names retrieved through knowledge base. 
- Please carry out this upgrade using appropriate ```ALIAS``` and ```Version``` of the Agent you created in Task2.
- ⚠️ Don't close window of Bedrock Agent prompt until you have created the Codedeploy Deployment infrastructure completely, as if session is closed it will not remember anything and start from begining.
- Try to validate the parameters being passed on to specific tool, if you face any error as sometime it may try to pick it up on its own but try to see the ```Show Trace``` and troubleshoot it.
- Please wait for 5 minutes for the Deployment to get rolled out, you can monitor it in CodeDeploy under Deployment, and then click on ```Check My Progress``` once it gets completed.
- If incase by mistake you created an appsec file with wrong values, you can rerun and create a new ```Appsec``` file as versioning is enabled it always picks up latest file. After that you can release the deployment once again. 

## Services You Should Use
- **Amazon Bedrock Agent** 
- **AWS Lambda**
- **AWS CodeDeploy**

## Task Validation
You have permissions to view the Deployments under CodeDeploy Service once its rolled out with specific configurations using UpgradeRollOut Agent. And view the Blue/Green Deployment being carried out by CodeDeploy. Once its Succeeded try to click on ```Check My Progress``` it should validate and complete the task. Validation function also takes into consideration the name of the configuration so try to give exact names.

### Background
You are a Cloud Engineer at Blace Software Labs, a company embracing AI-powered cloud management. The CTO has tasked you with streamlining database upgrades using cutting-edge AI technology. Your mission is to leverage AWS Strands Agent to automatically identify and modify specific RDS instances, demonstrating the power of AI in cloud operations. Before you can build and use your AI Agent, you certainly want to implement security guardrails to prevent harmful actions in AI operations, protecting your infrastructure from unintended modifications. 

### Your Task
Create and configure a Guardrail in Amazon Bedrock that you will later apply to your AI agent. The guardrail will define word filters based on custom words and phrases that prevent harmful operations such as database deletions.

Reference Documentation: For detailed guidance on creating guardrails in Amazon Bedrock, refer to the [Amazon Bedrock User Guide - Create your guardrail](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-components.html)

### Getting Started
To create the guardrail and deploy a version of the guardrail, follow these general steps:

1. Download [blocked_phrases.txt](https://aws-jam-challenge-resources.s3.amazonaws.com/ai-cloud-engineer-assistant/blocked_phrases.txt) file and save it on your computer locally. Remember the location of the file, as you will need this file to create the guardrail.
2. Navigate to the AWS Management Console
3. Access the Amazon Bedrock service
4. Find the Guardrails and then click on "Create guardrail"

    Use the following information for the fields in the "Provide guardrail details" page:
- **Name**: Jam-AI-Agent-Guardrail
- **Description**: Provide safeguards for AI Agent to prevent harmful content, protect user privacy, ensure factual accuracy, and prevent any harmful operations such as deleting resources.
- **Messaging for blocked prompts**: Sorry, I am not allowed to perform this action or answer the question. That's a guardrail by AWS Jam.
- Leave all other settings default and click next.

    Configure the remaining steps:
- In the next 2 steps, leave all default/disabled
- **Add word filters**: 
  - Go to section "Add custom words and phrases"
  - Select "Upload from a local file" and upload your downloaded blocked_phrases.txt
  - Review uploaded phrases in the *View and edit words and phrases* list
  - Click next, keep remaining steps default/disabled
- On the final step click "Create guardrail"

6. Once you have created "Jam-AI-Agent-Guardrail", create a version:
   - Create new version
   - Set "Version 1" in the "Description - optional" field
7. **Important**: Find and copy the ID value from the Guardrail Overview section. You'll need this ID for task validation and Task 3.

### Inventory
- Amazon Bedrock – Guardrails
- blocked_phrases.txt file

- Amazon Bedrock

1. Instruct the agent to modify the instance class of tagged databases
1. Ensure the changes are applied immediately

### Getting Started

## Background

BananaCode's LangGraph workflow is the brain of the code review system, designed to execute a sequence of states: fetch → analyze → validate → approve/reject. However, the workflow is currently broken and skips the critical "analyze" state, routing all code directly to approval without proper review. As of now, the system automatically approves all submitted code regardless of quality, but it should intelligently reject low-quality code and only approve code that meets quality standards production.

challengeTitle: The AI Legal Analyst: Optimized RAG with liteLLM Unified Interface
content:
# Challenge Overview

You are a newly-promoted AI Architect at Juris AI, a top-tier law firm staking its future on generative AI. Your mandate is to build a system that is powerful, cost-effective, and exceptionally agile. The firm's strategy is to always use the best model for the job, whether it's from Amazon Bedrock, a SageMaker endpoint, or another leading provider.
To achieve this, you will architect an optimized RAG system that uses liteLLM as a universal interface. By embedding liteLLM's SDK wrapper in your code, you can create a single, consistent way to call any model. This unified interface will allow Juris AI to intelligently route queries to the best Bedrock model for a given task, while ensuring the flexibility to integrate new models from any provider in the future—all without rewriting the core application logic. Your mission is to configure this sophisticated system, from the routing logic to the final security checks.

## Task 1: Architecting the Universal Model Map

### Background

It's your first strategy meeting with the CIO, Ana Carolina Silva. She's excited about the project. "I'm reading about new models being released every month," she says. "Some are better at summarization, others at complex reasoning. How do we build a system that can adapt and always leverage the best tools on the market? I want our firm to have that agility." You smile, ready for this question. "That's precisely why we're using a universal interface," you explain. "Our application code makes a single, standardized call through the liteLLM library. Your first task is to create the central 'control panel' for this system—a configuration that tells liteLLM which model to use for which job, giving us the power to change our model strategy on the fly."

### Inventory

The following resources have been created for this task:

- DynamoDB table named **jam-riv25-ddb** with partition key set to "intent" and sort key set to "model_id"
- AWS Bedrock models already enabled in the account
- liteLLM library configured as a unified API interface

### Your Task

You need to configure the core routing logic for the liteLLM interface by creating intent-to-model mappings in a DynamoDB table. Each intent represents a different level of reasoning required, and is mapped to a model from the Nova family that best matches its complexity. This setup ensures that simpler queries are routed to lighter models for efficiency, while more demanding queries leverage more capable models. The DynamoDB table uses the `intent` as the partition key and the AWS Bedrock model identifier (prefixed with `bedrock/`) as the `model_id` sort key, following liteLLM’s routing requirements.

The three possible values for the `intent` partition key are:

- `summarize-fast` - for quick document summaries
- `interpret-deep` - for complex legal analysis
- `extract-balanced` - for balanced information extraction

The three models you should consider are from the Nova family (Pro, Lite and Micro). Use their specific AWS Bedrock model identifiers for the `model_id` sort key, prefixed with `bedrock/`. liteLLM requires this prefix for routing, check out examples from their docs [here](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/providers/bedrock).

This configuration will serve as the strategic foundation of the entire multi-model system, allowing for instant changes without any code deployment.

Before you begin, also verify that you are in the `us-east-1` (N. Virginia) region.

### Getting Started

Navigate to the AWS Console and ensure you are in the N. Virginia region. The DynamoDB table has already been created for you.

### Services You Should Use

- Amazon DynamoDB

### Task Validation

The validation Lambda Function will make API calls to the DynamoDB table with intents and expects the corresponding model_IDs as response. The system will verify that all three intent mappings have been correctly configured.

## Background

A junior paralegal, Mateo Jackson, flags you down in the hallway. "I tried the new AI tool," he says. "I just asked it to find a date on a contract, and it felt like I was using a sledgehammer to crack a nut. The answer was right, but it took a moment." You realize the system is using one of its most powerful and sophisticated models for every single query, regardless of complexity. It's time to implement a "triage" step. Your job is to teach the system how to think before it acts.

## Inventory

The following resources have been created for this task:

- Lambda function (`jam-riv25-task-2-function`) with liteLLM library layer pre-installed
- Function code with a placeholder for your system prompt
- Test event capability in Lambda console

## Your Task

You need to transform a fast, inexpensive Amazon Nova Micro model into an expert "intent classifier" by engineering an effective system prompt. This Lambda function will serve as the application's single entry point, intercepting every user query to determine its nature and provide the appropriate routing key.

Your prompt engineering challenge is to instruct the model to analyze incoming queries and classify them into one of three categories, responding with only the exact classification string:

- `summarize-fast` for summarization requests
- `interpret-deep` for analysis and interpretation requests
- `extract-balanced` for information extraction requests

This demonstrates a production pattern where a cheap model handles initial processing (like triage) to determine if a more expensive model is needed for the main task.

## Getting Started

Navigate to the AWS Lambda console and locate the pre-configured Lambda function.

## Services You Should Use

- Amazon Lambda
- Amazon Bedrock

## Task Validation

Your implementation will be validated by testing the Lambda function with various query types. The function must return exactly one of the three classification strings (`summarize-fast`, `interpret-deep`, or `extract-balanced`) with no additional text. Test your implementation with queries such as:

- "Please provide a summary of the main legal points"
- "What does this clause mean and why is it important?"
- "List all the dates mentioned in this agreement"

## Background

You're in the final project review with the firm's Chief Legal Officer. They're pleased but have one critical concern. "I have nightmares about an attorney accidentally pasting a client's personal information into a query and that data being logged. A single PII breach could be catastrophic. What's our final line of defense?" You assure them that a powerful tool requires an equally powerful, built-in gatekeeper.

You will implement a non-negotiable layer of security using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. While the liteLLM library in your Lambda function provides a unified interface for model access, the underlying Bedrock platform provides deep, integrated safety features. - Profanity filtering
- Complete PII detection and blocking for all 31 PII types
- Grounding and relevance checks

challengeTitle: ECS Blue to Green: Zero-Downtime Deployment
content:
### 📝 Background

Your first task is to modify the existing ECS service deployment configuration from Rolling Update to ECS Native Blue/Green deployment. Currently, the service is running with:

### 📚 Understanding ECS Native Blue/Green Deployment

With ECS native Blue/Green deployment:
- 🟢 New tasks (green) are launched with updated task definition
- 🔵 Original tasks (blue) continue serving traffic
- ⚖️ Traffic is shifted only when new tasks are healthy
- ↩️ Easy rollback by shifting traffic back to blue tasks
- 🗑️ Old tasks are terminated after successful deployment

> 📌 **Note**: For this deployment, we will not configure test traffic - focusing only on production traffic shift between blue and green environments.

### 🎯 Your Task

Update the ECS service deployment configuration:
 - Use Task Definition version 2 [New version contains green-themed webpage]

 - Configure termination timeout for old tasks
 - Set deployment configuration for traffic shifting

### 🛠️ Getting Started

2. Locate your service in the cluster
3. Update service deployment configuration
4. Trigger deployment with new task definition

taskTitle: Enable Deployment Protection with Circuit Breaker
content:
### 📝 Background

Great job on setting up _Blue/Green deployment!_ Now it’s time to strengthen your deployment process with deployment protection using the **ECS deployment circuit breaker**.

The development team has prepared version 3 of the web application, but they’re uncertain about its stability. **Without a circuit breaker**, failed deployments could leave your service in an unstable state. The circuit breaker automatically monitors the _deployment process, detects failures, and rolls back_ to the last stable version when needed — helping you achieve _zero-downtime and fail-safe deployments_.


### 🔄 Current State
- ✅ Blue/Green deployment is configured
- 🟢 Service is running with version 2 (green theme)
- ⚠️ Deployment protection is currently OFF
- 🚀 Version 3 needs to be deployed with protection

### 📚 Understanding Circuit Breaker

The ECS deployment circuit breaker:
- 🛡️ Monitors deployment health
- 🔍 Detects failed task launches
- ⚡ Identifies unstable service states
- ↩️ Enables automatic rollback

> 🔔 **Note**: Without deployment protection, failed deployments could leave your service in an unstable state.

### 🎯 Your Task

1. Enable the ECS deployment circuit breaker:
   - Update service with new task definition version 3
   - Turn on failure detection
   - Configure automatic rollback
   - Keep existing Blue/Green deployment settings

2. Deploy Task Definition version 3:
   - Let circuit breaker monitor the deployment
   - Verify protection is working

### 🛠️ Getting Started

1. Navigate to the ECS Console
2. Locate your service in the cluster
3. Update service deployment configuration
4. Trigger deployment with new task definition


### 📦 Inventory

**ECS Service Current Configuration:**

- Service Name: web-service
- Current Task Definition: tech-corp:2 (stable green version)
- New Task Definition: tech-corp:3 (to be deployed)
- Deployment Protection: Disabled


**Load Balancer Details:**

ALB DNS: techcorp-alb-12345678.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com

### 💡 Services You Should Use
- Amazon ECS

### ✅ Task Validation

Your task will be validated in two phases:

**Phase 1 - Configuration Check:**
- Deployment circuit breaker is enabled
- Automatic rollback is configured
- New deployment of version 3 starts

**Phase 2 - Protection Verification:**
- ⏳ Wait for deployment to progress
- 🔄 Monitor service stability
- ⚠️ If failures occur, wait for threshold to be reached
- ✅ Verify automatic rollback to version 2

### 🔍 Monitoring Steps

1. **Watch Deployment Progress:**

Initial State    →    Deployment Started    →    Waiting Period    →    Final State
(Version 2)         (Version 3 deploying)     (Monitoring Phase)     (Rollback or Success)

2. **Key Indicators to Monitor:**
   - Service Events in ECS Console
   - Task Health Status
   - Deployment State Changes
   - Rollback Triggers

3. **Success Scenarios:**
   - Either: Version 3 deploys successfully
   - Or: Automatic rollback to Version 2 after failure threshold reached

> ⚡ **Important**: Do not manually intervene during the waiting period. Let the circuit breaker do its job!

### ⏱️ Expected Timeline

Deployment Start → [2-3 minutes] → Threshold Check → [5-10 minutes] → Auto Rollback

### 🎯 Validation Complete When:
- Circuit breaker has been triggered
- Automatic rollback has completed
- Service returns to stable state with Version 2
- All events are logged in ECS console


### 📚 Additional Resources

[ECS Deployment Circuit Breaker Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/deployment-circuit-breaker.html)

> ⚠️ **Important**: Once configured, the circuit breaker will automatically detect and respond to deployment issues. No manual intervention needed!

Need help? Use the clues below! 👇

content:

## Background

**Acme Online**, an e-commerce company, is implementing an automated solution to categorize their product images using AWS services. This system aims to replace their manual categorization process, which is time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies.

## Task

Your e-commerce company, Acme Online, has set up the initial components of an automated product image categorization system using AWS services. The key components of this solution include:

* **Amazon S3 bucket** (with prefix "product-categorization") to store all product images
* **AWS Lambda function** named "product-categorization-function" designed to process and categorize images
* **Amazon Rekognition** for image classification
* **Amazon DynamoDB** to store the categorization results

However, the system is not functioning as expected. Users are uploading files to the Amazon S3 bucket, but the AWS Lambda function is not being triggered automatically. As an engineer, you need to ensure that when files are uploaded to S3, the Lambda function is automatically triggered to process these images.

## Services to use
* Amazon S3
* AWS Lambda


## Inventory

* The AWS Lambda function named `product-categorization-function` is already created.
* An S3 bucket with the prefix "product-categorization" is set up to receive product images.

## Workflow:
* User uploads image to S3 bucket
* S3 bucket should trigger Lambda function (but currently not happening)
* Lambda function should process the image
* Amazon Recogniton will Catagorize the item
* DynamoDB table will be populated with new item along with catagorization details.


**Note:** You have permissions to modify S3 bucket settings and Lambda function configurations, but you cannot modify the Lambda function code or IAM policies.

## Getting Started

Review the existing `S3 bucket` (with prefix "product-categorization")  configuration and `Lambda function` settings.
Identify why the `Lambda function` is not being triggered when `new files` are uploaded to `S3`.
Implement a solution to ensure the Lambda function is automatically triggered by S3 uploads.
Test the updated solution by uploading new product images to the `S3 bucket` and verifying that the `Lambda function` is triggered.

## Validation
The task will automatically complete once you find a solution.

In this task, you need to deploy and launch the "App Factory" application, an innovative development platform integrated with Amazon Bedrock.

1. Build and launch "App Factory" by running the following commands:
   ```bash
   cd /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/app-factory-on-bedrock
   docker build . -t jam-server
   docker run -d -p 8080:8080 jam-server
   ```
   **Note:** The build step takes a few minutes to complete.
1. Open the `AppFactoryWebUrl` in the browser, which can be found from `Output Properties` in JAM Console, with the format `https://[sagemaker-notebook-name].notebook.[region].sagemaker.aws/proxy/8080/`
	- Screen shot:

		![Step1-screenshot](https://aws-jam-challenge-resources.s3.amazonaws.com/app-factory-on-bedrock/app-factory-step1.png)

## Services You Should Use
- Amazon SageMaker Notebook
- Docker

## Task Validation
Copy & paste you App Factory Web Url into JAM answer box

-----
## Read more

### Details about App Factory Application

This "App Factory" encompasses four key components: requirement analysis, code implementation, application deployment, and result review. 
1. In the requirement analysis module, you can engage in a conversation with an advanced Large Language Model (specifically Amazon Nova Lite in this case) to transform your app requirements into a comprehensive and detailed Product Requirements Document (PRD).
1. Through interaction with the LLM (as mentioned above), you can refine the app implementation details, such as button styles, font colors, and other design elements. 
1. The code deployment module allows you to deploy the results to AWS cloud, utilizing S3 for storing web files and CloudFront (CDN) to accelerate content distribution.
1. Moreover, if you wish to adjust any aspects of the application, you can always revert to the previous requirement analysis or code implementation steps at any time, ensuring flexibility throughout the development process.

#### Architecture

Here's the architecture for the "App Factory" application:

![](https://aws-jam-challenge-resources.s3.amazonaws.com/app-factory-on-bedrock/arch-app-factory.png)

In this architecture, we'll use the SageMaker Notebook instance to launch the "App Factory" and listen on port 8080. We'll then make it accessible through SageMaker's built-in proxy endpoint, i.e., the "/proxy/8080/" path.

**Note:** The SageMaker Notebook instance has already been provisioned, you don't have to create a new one.

challengeTitle: Only Authenticated Users can use the App
content:
## Overview

All you know is that you need to add a new user directory for the web application. You 
could take the endeavor of building your own user directory application and then adding
your own authentication page to the web application. However you need to keep in mind
that you will need to manage this application in the future. 

After sitting down with the product owner they gave you a few requirements that may
help you select the appropriate tool:
* Deliver frictionless customer identity and access management (CIAM) with a 
cost-effective and customizable platform.
* Add security features such as adaptive authentication, support compliance, and data 
residency requirements.
* Scale to millions of users across devices with a fully managed, high-performant, and 
reliable identity store.

## Your tasks
1. Find an AWS service that will meet the requirements described.
1. Configure that service with the following settings:
   * Only an **email** should be used to sign-in.
   * **Multi-factor authentication** is **not required** at this time.
   * The **user pool name** is not important for the product owner.
   * The **Cognito Domain** should be a unique value 
   * The **app client name** is not important for the product owner.
   * The web application being a single-page application only has one URL that will be used
for accessing it and for any kinds of **callback**. The **URL** for the web application can be 
found in the **Output Properties** on the left side of this screen under `WebApplicationURL`.
1. At this moment, all allowed users should be part of one **Group** and that group will provide
access to the **IAM role** that can be found in the **Output Properties** on the left side
of this screen under `CognitoGroupRoleName`. Users should be manually assigned to this
group when they are allowed to use the web application.

## Useful information
* If the setting isn't referred in the list of tasks, it probably means that it should be left
as the default value.
* The Callback URL must start with `https://` and end with `/`.
* You can try any entry in the answer field to receive guidance if you make a mistake.
* The error message of `Failed to fetch ACM certificates` at the top of the page while creating
the resource described above can be ignored.

## Task validation 
Once you complete the task, enter the `User pool ID` of the Cognito user pool you created to 
claim the points.

challengeTitle: Only Authenticated Users can use the App
content:
## Overview
Now that you have a user directory for external users that will allow them to
self-register. You need to integrate your new user directory with the current
service used to exchange user credentials for AWS credentials (access key, 
secret access key, session token) that are tied to the IAM role that you know 
so much about.

You know that this service is already in use for the internal users and that
they have access to a different IAM role. What you want to make sure is that
these external users only get the IAM role that has been assigned to them and
that there's no way any *default IAM role* would be associated with them. This
is so that you have to manually add the permission to those users once they
self-register.

Also, your CISO doesn't want any non-authenticated users to be able to access
the application so there shouldn't be any *Guest access*.

## Your tasks
1. Integrate your new user directory (**Identity provider**) with this service
and make sure that the IAM role is **selected** via the **preferred_role claim** 
that will be passed in the token generated by your new user directory. If the IAM 
role isn't passed in the token, then the **request** of this user should 
be **denied**.

## Useful information
* If the setting isn't referred in the list of tasks, it probably means that it 
should be left as the default value.
* You can click on the `Check my progress` button to check now and receive guidance 
if you made a mistake.

## Task validation
Once you complete the task, the task will be automatically validated.

challengeTitle: Only Authenticated Users can use the App
content:
## Overview

With the new user directory integrated with the AWS service used to exchange user
credentials with AWS credentials the last remaining step is to configure the web
application to use the new user directory.

The authentication flow should be the following:
1. Redirect the unauthenticated user to the Cognito user pool Hosted UI.
1. The user will login or create an account and login within the Hosted UI.
1. Once authenticated, the user will be redirected to the web application with a
`code` in the URL.
1. The `code` will be exchanged for Json Web Tokens (JWT) by calling the API of the
Cognito user pool hosted UI of `/oauth2/token` by sending a POST while supplying the
`code` and `app client id`. The API will provide access, id and refresh tokens, but 
only the `id_token` will be kept in the session storage and the user will be redirected
to the same web application page without the `code` in the URL.
1. The `id_token` from Cognito user pool that's now in the session storage will be sent 
to the Cognito identity pool API specifying the `user pool id` in exchange for AWS 
credentials associated with the IAM role that's supplied in the `id_token` claim. An 
access key, secret access key and session token will be in the response.

With AWS credentials now the web application can be used to upload files to S3 and
add items in DynamoDB as usual.

You spoke of the work you would have to do, in particular the authentication flow steps,
with a developer mentioning how much time this would take you to create all of that code 
in JavaScript. That developer mentioned that it would literally take them 5 minutes to 
code all of that. Taking this opportunity to reduce your workload you challenged that
developer to prove it.

Unfortunately, the developer caught on your scheme before finishing the work to integrate
their code modification with your new user directory configuration. That developer was
nice enough not to delete the entire code and said the modifications were done directly in
the web application already also telling you they wouldn't help you understand what was done. 
Hopefully there's some comments that can help you out in that code...

## Your tasks
1. Make sure the User Pool Domain Branding is **Hosted UI (classic)** and not **Managed login** as mentioned in *Task 1*.
1. Find where the developer left the code for the web application. All you know is the URL
of the web application which can be found in the **Output Properties** on the left side of
this screen under `WebApplicationURL`. The URL may give you a clue as to what service is
used to host such web application.
1. Inspect the code to see if you can find some **PLACEHOLDER** that were left by the
developer to integrate with your **User Pool Id**, your **User Pool App Client Id** and
the **User Pool Domain** that you created.
   * Only one file can and should be modified.
   * The developer may have left some examples of what those placeholder should be.
1. You will need to create an account to be able to use the web application.
1. Remember that only a certain **Group** is allowed to use the web application and that
you must manually add users to that group. This means that you may receive an error message
that your user isn't able to authenticate to the identity pool. You will need to use the
`Logout` and `Login` button again to be able to get new credentials.
1. Once you successfully upload a file via the web application, you will receive the answer
for this challenge.

## Useful information
* You need to use the `Logout` button and then the `Login` button on the web application
to try your credentials again with the identity pool.
* The web application is composed of only 4 files.
* You can't modify 3 of the 4 files.
* You don't need to add any code.
* You will need to use a valid email address to be able to validate it. Any email provided will only be used for notification purposes in this Jam challenge.
* You can try any code to receive guidance if you make a mistake. 
* The web application also provides useful information if you make a mistake.
* If you needed to revert back one of the files, note that versioning is turned on. This
should not be necessary unless you made a mistake.

## Task validation
Once you complete the task, you will receive a code to enter as the answer to claim the points
of this challenge.

content:
### Background
Recall from the communication that the Security Consultant in your company wants you to put restrictions on your GenAI-based application to provide responses to the users only from the data which corresponds to their department. Lets first make yourself familar with the architecture and data flow.
<br /><img src="https://aws-jam-challenge-resources.s3.amazonaws.com/authorize-your-agents/LLM%20application%20data%20authorization-Page-1.drawio.png" alt="SlotValue" width="700" height="450" />


### Your Task
Now that you understand the Architecture diagram and how different AWS services are interacting with each other, you want to analyze the problem. WAIT! Some pieces of this application are still not built, so let's first connect the missing parts and identify the problem.

As part of this task, create the AWS Bedrock Knowledge Base and link it with the existing S3 Data Source to convert it into embeddings and store in a vector database. This knowledge base will be used as a data source for your application to curate responses for your queries.

As part of the GenAI application following infrastructure has been provisioned for your already.

3. Amazon Lambda

### Getting Started
Please follow below steps
- Create a self-managed unstructured vector store AWS Bedrock Knowledge Base with the name `myknowledgebase`. 
- Select the exisitng IAM role as `AmazonBedrockExecutionRoleForKnowledgeBase`.
- Configure your Data Source as Amazon S3. Select the bucket <code>application-data-bucket-</code>.
- Choose the Embedding Model to convert the natural language data in the S3 bucket into embeddings. You need to choose the `Titan Text Embedding V2` model in this case. Embedding is the numerical representation of your text data.

- After the creation of Knowledge Base you need to <b>`SYNC`</b> it with data source.


### Links to follow

content:
#### Background
You have become familiar with the Application Architecture and connected several key components. In this task, you'll integrate the final missing component, bringing your chatbot application to completion.

#### Your Task
The objective of this task is to test the Amazon Lex chatbot by submitting a specific query and analyzing its response.

To achieve this objective, you need to integrate AWS Lambda function with the Knowledge Base you have created in Task 1.

For this challenge, App Users and their respective Departments have been pre-configured in Amazon Cognito.
You will assume the role of app user `jsmith` from the `HR` department.


##### Important Context
In a real-world scenario, User logs in with credentials (username/password), which verifies it's identity and returns JWT tokens. When user makes an API request, they include the JWT token in the Authorization header. The token's information is used to identify user roles and assign appropriate permissions.

For this challenge, we have implemented a simplified approach where users are pre-configured in Amazon Cognito with their respective department groups (HR or Finance). Instead of traditional password-based authentication and JWT token generation, the `department-validation` Lambda function simply queries Cognito to check which group the user belongs to. We recommend reviewing the AWS Cognito user configuration and examining the lambda function `department-validation` for additional insights.

#### Inventory
The following resources have been provisioned for you to successfully attempt the challenge.
- Amazon Lex
- Amazon Lambda
- Amazon Cognito

#### Services you should use
- Amazon Lex
- Amazon Lambda

#### Getting Started
Please follow below steps
1. Retrieve the Knowledge Base ID from `myknowldgebase` created earlier.
2. Input this ID into the environment variable of the Lambda function (identified by `find-secretkey-lambda`) that will be integrated with the Knowledge Base and Lex chatbot.
3. Navigate to Lex Console, click on bot with name `InternalBot`-> Click on `Intent` option from the left pane -> Press `Build` button(on top right) and wait for build to be completed sucessfully.
4. To initiate the Chat, Click `Test` Button (top right) and Submit the query: `What is my Secret Key?` to get the response by following the instructions.
5. Have you noticed an unexpected behavior in the Lex Chabot response? The ability to access keys from departments other than your own (Finance in this scenario). This represents a critical Data Authorization issue that needs to be addressed.
6. Paste the Finance department secret key in Submit Answer to complete the task.

#### Links to follow

- Testing a Amazon Lex Chatbot via Console - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lexv2/latest/dg/test-bot.html

challengeTitle: Control your data in Gen AI applications
content: #### Background In the previous step, you have completed the setup of your application but you have witnessed the problem of Data Confidentiality breach by having the access to other's Department Secret keys. This is the real problem you need to solve. ##### The Solution: Metadata Filtering To resolve this security challenge, we'll implement the `Metadata Filtering` approach that ensures: - Precise data identification within your S3 bucket - Strict access controls - Secure, context-aware information retrieval ##### How Metadata Filtering Works - Attach unique metadata tags to each document - Match user queries against document metadata - Retrieve only documents matching the user's department and access level #### Your Task Upload department-specific metadata files in respective HR and Finance folders. It will help in precisely identifing and restricting file access based on user context #### Inventory The following resources have been provisioned for you to successfully attempt the challenge. - Amazon S3 - Amazon Lambda #### Services you should use - Amazon S3 #### Getting Started Please follow below steps 1. As a first step, download the two Metadata file from the provided link. - Finance department metadata file - finance.txt.metadata.json - HR department metadata file - hr.txt.metadata.json - Use `Save as` to download the files and save on your local laptop. 2. `finance.txt.metadata.json` - Upload it in the `Finance` folder of the S3 bucket application-data-bucket-. 3. `hr.txt.metadata.json` - Upload it in the `HR` folder of the S3 bucket application-data-bucket-. 4. `SYNC` your Bedrock Knowledge Base again with the new data sets you have uploaded in data source S3 bucket. #### Links to follow - How to upload object in S3 bucket - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/upload-objects.html. #### Task Valdation This task will be vaildated once these files are uploaded in their respective folder & knowledge base is synced.

challengeTitle: Control your data in Gen AI applications
content:
#### Background Feeling tired? Don't worry! You've made great progress and now at the most exciting stage of this challenge. In the previous step, you successfully uploaded metadata files to the HR and Finance folders in the S3 bucket. #### Your Task Here is your target Architecture to achieve in this task. What difference did you found when compared with intial Architecture in Task 1? You got it absolutely correct!! The `secret-key-lambda` is now replaced with `metadata-filter-lambda`. In this task, you will replace the exising lambda function with new lambda function `metadata-filter-lambda` to attach with Amazon Lex chatbot and Bedrock Knowledge Base.
But Wait! Did you checked the new Lambda function? Below is the Code snippet which is making the difference. 

# Define retrieval configuration inline
  retrieval_configuration = {
    "vectorSearchConfiguration": {
        "filter": {
            "equals": {
                "key": "group",
                "value": department
              }
         }
     }
  }

  bedrock_runtime = boto3.client('bedrock-agent-runtime')
  response = bedrock_runtime.retrieve(
     knowledgeBaseId=os.environ['KNOWLEDGE_BASE_ID'],
     retrievalQuery={
        'text': event['inputTranscript']
     },
     retrievalConfiguration=retrieval_configuration
  )
This code dynamically appends metadata to user queries by identifying the user's department in the retrieval configuration. By applying a metadata filter, it restricts the search to only those documents in the Knowledge Base's vector database that match the specified departmental context, ensuring precise and targeted information retrieval. #### Inventory The following resources have been provisioned for you to successfully attempt the challenge. - AWS Lambda function - Amazon Lex - Amazon S3 #### Services you should use - Amazon Lex - Amazon Lambda #### Getting Started Please follow these steps: 1. Attach a new lambda function `metadata-filter-lambda` with the Lex chatbot. Click on your Lex Bot -> From left pane select `Alias` as `TestBotAlias` and click on Languages as `English`-> Choose the `metadata-filter-lambda` lambda from the drop-down and click Save. 2. Retrieve the Knowledge Base ID from `myknowldgebase` created in Task 1. 3. Set the Knowledge Base ID into the environment variable of the Lambda function (metadata-filter-lambda) to integrate with the Knowledge Base. 4. Test your query again. Go to Lex Console -> Intent -> Test(on top right) to open the Lex chat box. Type a query `What is my Secret Key`. Follow the response to get your Secret Key. 5. Paste the HR department key in Input box. You should now notice a difference in the chat response - you'll only see the SECRET KEY that belongs to your department. This challenge demonstrates how to use the powerful Metadata Filtering feature to segregate data in environments with users having different roles and responsibilities. This helps achieve Data Authorization control. #### Links to follow - How to Attach a Lambda with Lex chatbot - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lexv2/latest/dg/lambda-attach-console.html#:~:text=You%20must%20first%20attach%20a,language%20supported%20by%20the%20bot. #### Task Valdation This task will be validated automatically once you successfully update the new Lambda to the Amazon Lex chatbot & paste the Key in Submit Answer box. challengeTitle: Build an Automated ML Pipeline with Amazon SageMaker
content:
## Background

After executing a `SageMaker Pipeline`, various artifacts are generated and stored in the default `SageMaker S3 bucket`. These artifacts contain crucial information about data preprocessing, model training, evaluation results, and model registration. Understanding and analyzing these evaluation metrics is essential for assessing model performance. While these evaluation results are stored in `S3`, `SageMaker` also provides convenient programmatic access to these metrics through its API. Instead of manually retrieving and parsing files from `S3`, we can access the evaluation results directly using the `SageMaker SDK`. This programmatic approach is more efficient, and can be easily integrated into workflows and reporting systems. In this context, we'll demonstrate how to retrieve and analyze evaluation metrics programmatically from a SageMaker Pipeline execution.

## Inventory
  - `Model evaluation artifacts`
 

## Your Task

Obtain and Analyze the Evaluation Results

## How to Start
1. Upon successful completion of the pipeline execution, run `Step 4. Observe the evaluation metrics` in `pipeline-challenge.ipynb`

Note: This process typically takes 1-2 minutes. The wait time ensures proper retrieval and processing of all necessary evaluation data from the AWS infrastructure.
The delay in output is normal and occurs because the code is performing several sequential API calls to AWS services:
First, it queries `SageMaker` to list pipeline executions
Then, it interacts with `S3` to:
List objects in the evaluation directory
Retrieve the actual evaluation file


2. Analyze the results

In regression problems like the abalone age prediction, two commonly used evaluation metrics are Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Standard Deviation (STD):

Mean Squared Error (MSE):
- Measures the average squared difference between predicted and actual values
- Lower MSE values indicate better model performance
- Heavily penalizes large errors due to squaring
- Always non-negative, with 0 being perfect prediction

Standard Deviation (STD):
- Measures the amount of variation or dispersion in predictions
- Calculated as the square root of the variance
- Indicates how spread out the predictions are from their mean
- Lower STD suggests more consistent predictions
- Useful for understanding prediction reliability and model stability

For the abalone age prediction problem, these metrics help us understand both the accuracy (MSE) and consistency (STD) of our model's predictions. The actual values of these metrics can vary significantly depending on the specific problem, data scale, and model performance. What constitutes a "good" MSE or STD is highly context-dependent.



## Services in Use
- `Amazon SageMaker`

## Task Validation
Enter the types (not values) of metrics from evaluation report, with metrics separated by a space
Example format: metric1 metric2

**Decision Criteria Reference**
Correct metrics from the evaluation report have been entered.

challengeTitle: Build an Automated ML Pipeline with Amazon SageMaker
content:
## Background

The `Model Registry` in `SageMaker` maintains versions of trained models and requires approval decisions based on model performance metrics. The approval process ensures only models meeting specific quality criteria are deployed to production. `Model lineage` tracking provides transparency and accountability in the ML lifecycle.

## Inventory
- `Model Registry` entry
- `Model version` details
- `Model evaluation metrics`:
  - `MSE (Mean Squared Error)`
  - `Standard Deviation`
- Approval status options:
  - `Approved`
  - `Rejected`

## Your Task
1. Review model version details in `Model Registry`
2. Analyze model `evaluation metrics`
3. Make approval decision based on criteria:
   - Approve if: MSE < 6 AND standard deviation < 3
   - Reject if: criteria not met

## How to Start
1. In `SageMaker Studio`, navigate to `Models`
2. Under `Registered Models` you will see the name of your model that was registered from the pipeline
`abalone-model-new-sdk`
3. Select this model and click on the `Model Version 1` (there should be only 1 version if you ran the pipeline once)
4. Under Overview there are 4 tabs:  `Train`, `Evaluate`, `Audit` and `Deploy` 
5. On the `Deploy` tab, click on `Pending Approval` 
6. Refer to the  evaluation metrics `MSE` and `standanrd Deviation` from the previous task 
7. Use the values of the `MSE` and `Standard Deviation` metrics from Task 3 to apply decision criteria
8. Make approval decision - Change from `Pending` to `Approved` or `Rejected` based on the metrics values

Model Status Actions:
If Approved: Pipeline continues to next steps (e.g., deployment)
If Rejected: Pipeline stops, preventing deployment of underperforming models

Note on Model Registry Versions and MLOps Best Practices:
In MLOps, model versioning through a Model Registry is a crucial practice for maintaining traceability and reproducibility. When working with SageMaker Pipelines, ach pipeline execution that results in a new model being registered creates a new version in the Model Registry. Versions are incremented sequentially (1.0, 2.0, etc.)

## Services in Use
- `Amazon SageMaker`
- `SageMaker Model Registry`


## Task Validation
Enter your approval decision: `Approved` or `Rejected` based on the evaluation criteria

**Decision Criteria Reference**

Approve/reject version 1 of the model based on the mse and deviation values from previous step)
- Approve if:
  - MSE < 6 AND
  - Standard Deviation < 3
- Reject if above criteria not met

## Background

A large enterprise customer is struggling with efficient log analysis, spending hours manually reviewing CloudWatch Logs for security incidents and operational issues. They need an automated solution that can provide quick, understandable insights from their log data. Your team has initiated development of an automated log analysis system using AWS services. The key components have been set up, but there are integration issues preventing the system from functioning properly. The existing components include:

## Task
As our AWS Bedrock implementation continues to evolve, we must ensure our Lambda function is optimally configured to handle various model interactions effectively. Recent performance analysis has revealed that the default Lambda configuration may not be sufficient for consistent and reliable model operations.

Our monitoring data indicates that some model interactions require additional processing time and memory resources, particularly when handling complex requests or when multiple API calls are needed across regions. To address this, our product team has conducted extensive testing and performance analysis.

Based on their findings, the optimal configuration has been determined:

Memory allocation should be increased to `256 MB` to ensure smooth processing of model responses
Timeout duration should be set to `60 seconds` to accommodate potential latency in cross-region API calls and model processing time
By implementing these recommended configurations, we can:

* Minimize the risk of function timeouts during critical operations
* Ensure consistent performance across different regions
* Maintain reliable model interaction capabilities
* Optimize cost-to-performance ratio for our serverless architecture
These adjustments will help establish a more robust and dependable foundation for our Bedrock implementation, ensuring smooth operations as we scale our AI/ML capabilities across different regions.

## Background

## Your Task

## Principle of Least Privilege
This Jam challenge is designed following the principle of least privilege. The principle of least privilege refers to the security best practice of granting users, systems, or processes only the minimum levels of access or permissions necessary to perform their required functions.

During the challenge you may encounter **AcccessDeniedException**. This is by design. Your account has the access needed to complete the challenge. If you're unable to proceed due to an AccessDeniedException please try a different solution to accomplish the task.

## Background

Now that CloudTrail is logging events to CloudWatch you are ready to capture the API calls causing the EC2 instances to stop. You just need to replicate the issue to generate the event and logs.

Continue investigating what is stopping the instance and **identify the resource** to complete this challenge. **The name of the resource is the answer to this challenge.**

## Getting Started

#### Start an EC2 instance
1. Go to the **Amazon EC2** service in the **AWS console** and select **Instances** from the navigation menu on the left.
1. From there you will see an EC2 instance in the `stopped` state. Attempt to start the instance by choosing the instance and selecting **Instance state > Start instance** and see what happens.

#### Analyze Log Data with CloudWatch Log Insights
1. Next, open the **CloudWatch** console at https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/
1. In the navigation pane, choose **Logs**, and then choose **Logs Insights**.
On the Logs Insights page, the query editor contains a default query that returns the 20 most recent log events.
1. In the **Select log group(s)** drop down, choose the `/aws/cloudtrail/jam-management-events` log group to query.

Additionally check if the Internet traffic is allowed in the outbound rule of the same Security Group.

taskTitle: Setup AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Agent on On-Premise server and registering it with the AWS Systems Manager service.
content:
**Background**

You are an employee at a multinational banking firm called **SampleBank**. As part of the hybrid cloud setup, your organization wants to access the AWS services from on-premises resources. To achieve this, the on-premises servers need IAM credentials.

After conducting some initial research, you have discovered the AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Agent, which can help you set up IAM credentials on the on-premises servers. You have taken the initiative to work on a Proof of Concept (POC) for this task, and your goal is to set up the SSM Agent on one of the on-premises servers.

To replicate the on-premises scenario, a separate subnet called the Isolated Subnet has been created. All instances launched within this subnet will be treated as on-premises servers.
1. The on-premises server is an EC2 instance named "OnPremiseInstance".
2. Another EC2 instance named "LocalCloudInstance" will be used as a tooling server to perform all the necessary actions.

**Your Task:**

1. Log in to the `OnPremiseInstance` using the following steps:

   a. Log in to the `LocalCloudInstance` using the SSM Connect Option(connect via `Session Manager`).

   b. SSH into the `OnPremiseInstance` using the credentials stored in the SSM Parameter Store, named "`/security/remoteuser/credentials`".

2. Retrieve the Systems Manager Hybrid activation credentials stored in the AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store under the parameter named `/hybrid-activation/info`.

3. Use those activation credentials to set up(Register) the AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Agent on the on-premises instance named `OnPremiseInstance`. After successful registration, restart the `amazon-ssm-agent` service. 

	**Note:**
	1. Use the below command to register the instance to Amazon SSM.
	
		`sudo -E amazon-ssm-agent -register -code {ActivateCode} -id {ActivateId} -region {AWSRegion} -y`
	2. You will have to restart the Amazon SSM Agent after execution of below command.

4. After the successful registration of the on-premises instance with AWS Systems Manager, you should be able to access AWS IAM credentials. You can validate this by running the `aws sts get-caller-identity --endpoint-url https://sts.{AWSRegion}.amazonaws.com --region {AWSRegion}` command.

**Note:**

1. Amazon SSM Agent has already been installed on the instance.
2. As `Sudo` has been used to setup `Amazon SSM Agent`, use `Sudo` to perform the actions such AWS CLI and other commands on the On-premise instance.


**Getting Started**
1. Open the AWS EC2 console and log in to the `OnPremiseInstance` as mentioned in Step 1.

**Inventory**
- AWS Systems Manager - Parameter Store
- AWS Systems Manager - Fleet Manager
- AWS Systems Manager - Hybrid Activations
- Amazon EC2

- AWS Systems Manager - Fleet Manager

**Task Validation**
The task will be automatically complete once you configure the SSM Agent successfully, and it is shown as `Online` in Fleet Manager in the AWS Systems Manager console. You can also check your progress by pressing the "Check my progress" button in the challenge details screen.

**Note:**
1. As the Root user is used to set up the `amazon-ssm-agent`, the Root user will have the AWS credentials configured.

Through this challenge, you will learn:

1. How to securely access on-premises resources from the cloud using the AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Agent.
2. Techniques for managing and retrieving IAM credentials stored in the AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store.
3. The process of registering on-premises instances with the AWS Systems Manager for hybrid cloud integration.
4. Validating the successful integration of on-premises resources with the AWS cloud environment.

Verify that the VPC has the necessary network settings, such as private subnets, route tables, and any required VPC Endpoints, to enable connectivity to the S3 service.

2. **Explore VPC Endpoints**: Consider setting up an S3 VPC Gateway endpoint within the isolated VPC. This would allow the on-premises instance to access the S3 service through a private connection within the VPC, bypassing the need for a direct internet connection.

By investigating these potential causes, you should be able to identify and resolve the issue that is preventing the on-premises instance from successfully accessing the S3 service, despite the IAM role having the appropriate permissions.

taskTitle: Issuing a New Certificate from the Private Certificate Authority for Validation
content:
**Background**

This task involves integrating on-premises applications with AWS using IAM Roles Anywhere, which requires issuing a new certificate from the "jam-private-certificate-authority" to validate the proof of concept (POC).

**Your Task**

The goal of this task is to issue a new certificate from the "jam-private-certificate-authority" to validate the proof of concept (POC) integration between your on-premises applications and AWS using IAM Roles Anywhere.

**Getting Started**
1. Access the home directory of the "remote-user" user and locate the "csr.pem" file containing the certificate signing request.

**Inventory**
- Amazon EC2
- `csr.pem` file containing the certificate signing request. This is required to issue a new certificate.
- AWS Private Certificate Authority (PCA) "jam-private-certificate-authority"

**Services you should use**
- AWS Private Certificate Authority (PCA)

**Task**
1. Issue a new certificate from the Private Certificate Authority using the following details:
   - Signing Algorithm: "SHA256WITHRSA"
   - Validity: 30 Days

2. After issuing the certificate in Step 1, a Certificate ARN will be generated.

3. Retrieve the certificate from the AWS Private Certificate Authority and store it in a file named "cert.pem" in the "remote-user" home path `(/home/remote-user)`.
   
**Note:** 
1. As `Sudo` has been used to setup AWS Credentials, use `Sudo` to perform the actions such AWS CLI and other commands on the On-premise instance.
1. As the server does **not** have `jq` installed, hence use native AWS CLI functionality to extract the certificate. **Append** the following command as needed to AWS CLI command to fetch the certificate.
```bash
   --query 'Certificate' --output text
```

content:
**Background**

As part of the ongoing effort to integrate on-premises applications with the AWS cloud using IAM Roles Anywhere, the next step involves obtaining temporary security credentials to access AWS resources.
To do so, we will need [`aws_signing_helper`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/credential-helper.html)  tool, which is used to retrieve the IAM credentials using IAM Roles Anywhere.

**Your Task**

1. Locate the `aws_signing_helper` tool in an S3 bucket with the prefix `hybrid-cloud-storage-{AWSRegion}-{AWSAccountId}`.
2. Download the `aws_signing_helper` tool to the current location and make it executable.
3. Use the `aws_signing_helper` tool to obtain the temporary security credentials, including an access key, secret key, and session token.
4. Use the temporary credentials to interact with the AWS Secrets Manager service and retrieve the value of the "JAMsecretmger" secret.

**Getting Started**

1. Log in to the on-premises instance as mentioned in Task #1.
2. Download the `aws_signing_helper` tool using the following command:
   ```bash
   aws s3 cp s3://bucket-name/aws_signing_helper . --region your-region
   chmod +x aws_signing_helper
   ```



**Inventory**
- [`aws_signing_helper`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/credential-helper.html) tool to get IAM Credentials
- The Certificate issued using ACM Private Certificate Manager in Task 4

- Private certificate file named `cert.pem`, present at `home` path of `remote-user`
- ARN of IAM Roles Anywhere Trust anchor, which has been created in Task 4.
- ARN of IAM Roles Anywhere Profile with name `JAM-RolesAnywhere-Profile`. This can be found in RolesAnywhere console.
- ARN of IAM Role "JAMIAMRolesAnywhereRole". This can be found in IAM Console.

**Services you should use**
- AWS Secrets Manager
- IAM Roles Anywhere

**Note:**
1. Use [`AWS CLI`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/secretsmanager/get-secret-value.html) to retrieve secret from AWS Secret Manager.
2. If you have exported the credentials without `Sudo` then use AWS CLI commands **without** `Sudo`.

**Task**
1. Execute the `aws_signing_helper` command to obtain the temporary security credentials.
2. Use the temporary credentials to interact with the AWS Secrets Manager service and retrieve the value of the "JAMsecretmger" secret.

**Task Validation**
1. Provide the value of the "JAMsecretmger" secret as the output.


By completing this task, you had successfully obtained the temporary security credentials and used them to access an AWS resource, demonstrating the seamless integration between your on-premises environment and the AWS cloud using IAM Roles Anywhere. This accomplishment brought you one step closer to achieving the overall goal of the proof of concept.
