Data preparation is the first and typically the most time-intensive phase of the ML workflow. Raw data often contains errors, inconsistencies, mising values and outliers. Data preparation involves cleaning the data to ensure its quality that is essential for the model's accuracy and reliability. Well-prepared data helps in efficient model training, faster convergence and improved performance. SageMaker Canvas offers comprehensive data preparation capabilities powered by [Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler](https://aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/data-wrangler/) in the SageMaker Canvas workspace. This enables you to go through all the phases of a standard ML workflow, from data preparation to model building and deployment, on a single platform. [Amazon SageMaker Canvas](https://aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/canvas/) is a low-code/no-code tool that provides a visual point-and-click interface for business analysts to solve business problems using Machine Learning without writing any code. In this challenge, you will build a multi-class classification model for predicting rank of a player based on the telemetry data available to you. You begin your journey to create a model by importing data within Sagemaker Canvas. The imported data is known as a Dataset within SageMaker Canvas. Amazon SageMaker Canvas supports importing tabular, image, and document data. Sagemaker Canvas allows you to import data from multiple data sources. However, for this exercise, you will use the data shared by your Data Analytics team in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) Bucket named "games-aiml-jam-sagemaker-data-${AWS::AccountId}-${AWS::Region}" in a file titled "GamesTelemetryData.csv"

Follow these steps to set up your dataset:

1. Go to Amazon SageMaker AI and Select Canvas under Applications and IDEs 2. Select user profile named ‘jam-ba-user' and click on 'Open Canvas'. Canvas will take a few minutes to load. 3. Create a new tabular dataset using gamestelemetrydata.csv. In the validation box above, enter the total cells in the dataset.

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the process of analyzing your data to identify trends, outliers and unexpected features. The results from this analysis are then used to make changes to your data, known as Feature Engineering. It can enhance model's predictive power, if done properly. SageMaker Canvas offers comprehensive data analysis and preparation capabilities powered by [Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler](https://aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/data-wrangler/) in the SageMaker Canvas workspace. SageMaker Data Wrangler includes built-in analyses that help you generate visualizations and data analyses in a few clicks. In this step, you will get additional insights on data and data quality using Quality and Insights Report and analyze Multicolinearity within data. Data Quality and Insights Report generates multiple insights from data like Duplicate rows, Anomalous samples and Prediction power of each feature. It also generates a Quick Model that can give you an idea of how your model will perform with the current dataset. Sagemaker Quick model splits the data into two subsets - training and validation data (in 80:20 ratio, customizable in advanced configurations). The training dataset is used to train the model while the validation dataset is used to test the model post training. Quick Model provides separate scores for each subset of data (Validation scores and Train scores) to provide you further insights into how the model can perform. Multicollinearity is a condition when there is a significant dependency or association between the predictor variables. Multicollinearity among data in a model can lead to inaccuracies and misleading results as they can overestimate impact of change in those predictor values on the target values. You can use the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), or Lasso feature selection as measures for the multicollinearity in your data. 1. The Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) is a measure of collinearity among variable pairs. Data Wrangler returns a VIF score as a measure of how closely the variables are related to each other. A VIF score is a positive number that is greater than or equal to 1. Higher the VIF score for a predictor variable, higher the correlation with other predictor variables. 2. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) measures the variance of the data along different directions in the feature space. The feature space consists of all the predictor variables that you use to predict the target variable in your dataset. From the feature space, PCA generates an ordered list of variances. These variances are also known as singular values. The values in the list of variances are greater than or equal to 0. You can use them to determine how much multicollinearity there is in your data. 3. Lasso feature selection uses the L1 regularization technique to only include the most predictive features in your dataset. A common feature selection method is to use all the features that have a non-zero lasso coefficient. L1 regularization can also help in addressing another common ML problem - Overfitting. Overfitting is a phenomenon that occurs when a Machine Learning model is constrained to the training set and not able to perform well on unseen data. You can detect presence of this problem by noticing significant difference between Validation and Train scores for your Model. To address overfitting, you remove features that have higher lasso co-efficient.

Follow these steps to perform Exploratory Analysis:

1. Create a new Data flow for your dataset. 2. Get Data Insights from the dataset by creating Data quality and Insights report (Hint: Target Column is "LeagueIndex"). Gather following insights: * First, how much "Missing Data" does the dataset have? It is common to have a small percentage of missing data. SageMaker Canvas, by default, replaces missing data with mean of other values for that variable. No additional action is needed unless you want to replace the missing values with some other value. * Second, are there any high priority warnings? * Third, are there duplicate rows in the dataset? SageMaker Canvas can remove those duplicates with visual workflow. * Fourth, how do Validation scores compare with Train scores in the Quick model? Significant difference between the two indicates potential case of overfitting in the model. You can use L1 regularization to address any observed case of overfitting. * Fifth, are there variables that have very low predicting power? Dropping them can make your model train faster. 3. Get additional Data Insights by creating a Multicollinearity report with the Variance Inflation Factors analysis type. Identify the variable which should be removed from this dataset. (If you do not see the column names in the chart, download the chart as png file and open the downloaded file to see the names of columns in the chart) 4. If L1 regularization is required, Create another Multicollinearity report with the Lasso feature selection analysis type. Identify the variable which should be removed from this dataset. (If you get unexpected internal error with "Lasso feature selection", create Multicollinearity report with type "Variation Inflation Factors" analysis type first and then change updated the report by changing type to "Lasso feature selection") 5. In the validation box above, enter the variables you have identified as needing to be removed from the dataset. (Enter each separated by a comma)

ML models are computer programs designed to learn from data, identify patterns and make predictions without being explicitly programmed to perform a specific task. Training a model involves selecting algorithms, adjusting parameters and evaluating model's performance in producing accurate results. Once trained, the program can use new, unseen data as input to generate predictions or classifications based on patterns it has learned during training phase. Amazon SageMaker Canvas allows you to quickly train, tune, and deploy models on the data that you've selected without writing any code. In the previous task, you identified the following variables that need to be dropped: * Drop column for Multicollinearity (vif) : uniqueunitsmade * Drop column for Multicollinearity (L1 regularization) : apm In this task, you will build a new Model to predict value of column "LeagueIndex" after applying the transformations listed above to the dataset. You can create the transformations in Data Flow itself and save the transformed dataset that can later be used to create the model. However, for this challenge, you will apply these transformations while creating a new Model.
Follow these steps:
1. On the left side, select 'My Models' and create a new Model. Deselect the columns above. 2. Click on the Quick Build button. 3. Wait for the build to complete. This will generally take 2-15 minutes. 4. Take a note of Accuracy of the recommended model. 5. Review other metrics for your model - Average f1, Average Precision and Average Recall 6. In the validation box above, enter the Average f1 of the model.
Congratulations! You have created a machine learning model!

Once you are satisfied with the model, you can deploy the model in Sagemaker Canvas itself to make it available for decision-making, prediction and insights. SageMaker provides the ML infrastructure for you to host your model on an endpoint with the compute instances that you choose. Then, you can invoke the endpoint (send a prediction request) and get a real-time prediction from your model.

Follow these steps:

1. Before trying to deploy, you need to confirm that you have the required privileges. 2. In the Sagemaker console, for jam_ba_user profile within AWS-Games-Jam-SageMaker-Domain domain, click Edit and make sure that "Enable direct deployment of Canvas models" toggle under Canvas settings is turned on. 3. Return to your model under My Models page in Sagemaker Canvas and Deploy it. 4. Please select Instance Type as "ml.m5.large" and Instance Count as 1 for testing purposes. Deploy the model and wait for it to become available, this will take a few minutes. 5. In the validation box above, enter the name of your deployment.

challengeTitle: Unified Data Querying with Amazon Athena
content:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) offers multiple storage solutions tailored to different aspects of game development. In this section, we will learn about those storage solutions and the purposes of using them to store game and player data.
**Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service):** S3 serves as an object storage service, ideal for storing game assets such as images and multimedia files along with formats like CSV, 3D models etc. Its scalability and ease of access make it a go-to choice for managing large binary data important for game development.
**Amazon DynamoDB:** DynamoDB is a NoSQL database service which can serve well in the real-time demands of gaming applications. Providing seamless scalability and low-latency access, it can be the backbone for managing dynamic player data, ensuring a responsive gaming experience.
**Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service):** RDS is a managed relational database service which simplifies the handling of structured data. With support for various database engines, it's the ideal solution for managing player profiles, game progress, and transactional data, ensuring a reliable foundation for game data management.

In order to efficiently store and retrieve large binary game assets, which AWS storage solution, is known for its scalability and object storage capabilities?

challengeTitle: Unified Data Querying with Amazon Athena
content:
**Amazon Athena** is a powerful and versatile querying tool. Whether your game data resides in S3, DynamoDB or RDS, Athena unifies the querying experience.
Athena empowers developers to write SQL-like queries opening the door to extracting meaningful insights and analytics across data sources.
As part of this task, we have created a datasource, database and a table based on sample data stored in S3. 1. Navigate to the [AWS Console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/console/home) 2. Locate the S3 bucket *games-simple-query/ranked-games-s3*, containing a file named "high_diamond_ranked_10min.csv". This is a csv file containing first 10 mins stats of a large number of ranked games.
3. Now, navigate to the Athena console. In the query editor, find the saved queries and run the query named **CreateTableFromS3Data**. Observe the table name, columns and data types in this query. Once this query is run, a new table is created in Athena that can be used to further retrieve data from S3.
- Note: Amazon Athena automatically stores query results and metadata information for each query that runs in a query result location that you can specify in Amazon S3. To set up an Amazon S3 query result location for the first time, see [Specifying a query result location using the Athena console](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/querying.html#query-results-specify-location-console) . Now, based on this data, you will perform the next step. Each row is a unique game and features have been collected after the first 10 mins of the game. Each game can be identified using a unique `gameId`. The row has another column `blueWins` that can be used to identify blue team's outcome. The values are 1 indicating win and 0 indicating lost.
Write a query to find the number of times Blue team won. Enter the number in the answer to complete this task.

With Athena Federated Query, you can run SQL queries across data stored in relational, non-relational, object, and custom data sources.

Preparing to create federated queries is a two-part process:
- Deploying a Lambda function data source connector, - Connecting the Lambda function to a data source. In this process, you give the Lambda function a name that you can later choose in the Athena console and give the connector a name that you can reference in your SQL queries.

taskTitle: Set an alarm to monitor for high model invocation latency
content:
# Background
Your organization has hosted an GenAI App through a web interface.
You are tasked to monitor the application stability through proper performance and usage monitoring.

When it comes to applications leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs), every millisecond counts and impacts the customer experience as they interact with the system. 

The speed and efficiency of LLM-powered responses can make or break user engagement and satisfaction.

# Getting Started
Navigate to the Challenge Outputs screen for this Jam Challenge (available on the left menu). Take note of the values for the following items. You will be using them to solve this challenge.
1. The Application URL - open this in a new browser tab or window.
This sample application invokes a Bedrock LLM (Amazon Nova Lite) to generate appropriate responses based on user prompts.

# Pre-Requisites
  Invoke Amazon Bedrock via the provided application interface to start generating metrics.
  
      1. First, navigate the to the Application URL you noted from the Challenge Outputs screen.
      2. In the application interface, test a few prompts by filling in the input field and clicking the `Invoke Bedrock` button.

# Your Task
The first task is to monitor the latency of the model output.
- Configure an Alarm to monitor the invocation latency of the 
amazon.nova-lite-v1:0 model and send notifications 
when it exceeds an acceptable threshold (>= 3000ms).
- The alarm should monitor over a timeframe of 15 minutes and send email notifications.

# Services You Should Use
- Amazon Cloudwatch Metrics
- Amazon CloudWatch Alarms
- Simple Notification Service (SNS)

# Task Validation
This task will be automatically marked as completed when:

1. A CloudWatch Alarm exists that will detect when the model invocation latency crosses a defined threshold (>=3000ms).
2. The CloudWatch Alarm is connected to an SNS topic.

Additionally, you can always check your progress by clicking on the Check my progress button on the Challenge Details screen.

# Important Information

You are using a training account with limited access to Amazon Bedrock. Due to the service quotas set for Requests per Minute (RPM), Tokens per Minute (TPM) and Tokens per Day (TPD) , you may encounter throttling issues. To mitigate these issues:

    Execute code blocks one at a time. If you receive an error, wait a few seconds before retrying.
    Avoid running multiple operations concurrently.
    If throttling persists, wait 2 minutes before running any code that interacts with Bedrock.
    If the problem continues after waiting, you may need to end the lab and start again.

We understand this is not ideal and are working hard to implement a permanent solution. Following these steps will help ensure a smoother experience as you explore Amazon Bedrock’s capabilities. In the interim, please provide the details of any problems you encounter using the https://support.aws.amazon.com/#/contacts/aws-training.

taskTitle: Set an alarm to monitor for high input token count
content:
# Background
In Task 1, we have setup an alarm to monitor for high invocation latency, now lets monitor for high token count.

A token comprises a few characters and refers to the basic unit of text that a model learns to understand the user input and prompt. With on-demand pricing models, you are charged for every input token processed.

High input token count can lead to higher costs, and in some cases result in invocation errors because the prompt is too long for requested model. We need your help creating a solution that will help us monitor for and alert when input token count exceeds a defined threshold.

# Getting Started
Navigate to the Challenge Outputs screen for this Jam Challenge (available on the left menu). Take note of the values for the following items. You will be using them to solve this challenge.
1. The Application URL - open this in a new browser tab or window

# Pre-Requisites

Ensure you've completed the pre-requisites as defined in Task 1.

# Your Task

Configure an alarm for high input token count
  - The alarm should trigger when the average of the tokens being utilized is greater than or equal (`>=`) to 2500 for the `amazon.nova-lite-v1:0` model.
  - The alarm should monitor over a timeframe of 15 minutes.

# Services You Should Use
- Amazon Cloudwatch Metrics
- Amazon CloudWatch Alarms
- Simple Notification Service (SNS)

# Task Validation
This task will be automatically marked as completed when:

1. A CloudWatch Alarm exists that will detect when the model input token count crosses a defined threshold (>= 2500ms).
2. The CloudWatch Alarm is connected to an SNS topic. **Hint:** you can reuse the SNS topic created in Task 1.

Additionally, you can always check your progress by clicking on the Check my progress button on the Challenge Details screen.

taskTitle: Set up a CloudWatch RUM application monitor
content:
# Background
Amazon CloudWatch RUM helps you monitor and improve your web application's performance by tracking real user interactions, page load times, and client-side errors. This data enables you to address performance issues, fix errors, and optimize the user experience based on actual user behavior.

In Task 1, we configured an alarm to monitor for high `InvocationLatency` which measures measures the time in milliseconds it takes for a model to process the prompt and generate a response. Since this is a server-side metric, it does not fully capture the impact on the client-side page load times, or factors like the network latency and the impact of multiple network hops.

# Inventory
1. An S3 bucket for hosting static website assets like JavaScript

# Getting Started
Navigate to the Challenge Outputs screen for this Jam Challenge (available on the left menu). Take note of the values for the following items. You will be using them to solve this challenge.

4. The RUM identity pool name

# Pre-Requisites
Confirm that you've configured access to the `Nova Lite` model as described in the Pre-Requisites section of Task 1.

# Your Task
We need you to take advantage of the CloudWatch RUM service to implement real user monitoring so we can understand the impact of high model invocation latency on our customers experience.

Create a CloudWatch RUM App Monitor and instrument the application:

- The app monitor should:
	- Have **Custom Events** enabled
	- Analyze 100% of sessions
	- In the authorization section, choose the option : Select existing identity pool.
	  Choose the `RumIdentityPool` from the dropdown selection.

Once the application has been instrumented, refresh your browser window with the application to ensure that the `cwrum.js` script is loaded. At this point, you can send some sample prompts and view the CloudWatch RUM events on the `Events` tab of the application monitor you configured earlier.

# Task Validation
This task will be automatically marked as completed when:

- A CloudWatch RUM application monitor has been created

challengeTitle: Unlocking Insights: Understanding the Voice of the Customer
content:
## Background:

In this task, you will deploy an application that allows you to listen to customer voices in multiple languages. You'll convert speech to text using [Amazon Transcribe](https://aws.amazon.com/transcribe/getting-started/?nc=sn&loc=4), an automatic speech recognition (ASR) service, to handle interactions with multiple customers simultaneously.

---

## Getting Started:

##### 1. Start up the Voice of Customer (VoC) Application:

- Copy paste `WebFileSyncApiGatewayInvokeURL` from **Output Properties**. (Ignore the SyntaxError)
- Get the `WebsiteURL` from **Output Properties** to access the VoC Application frontend. 
- Read the **Reference** section below to learn more about the Web Application.

##### 2. Configure the Backend API Endpoint:

- Locate `BackendApiEndpoint` value from **Output Properties** .
- Copy and Paste to the **Set Backend API** field on the WebUI.

Now you have a working VoC WebUI to process customer feedback.

However the "Start Transcription" botton is broken and you need to modify `VOCTranscribeFunction` Lambda function so it calls **Amazon Transcribe** to convert speech to text.


---

### Your Task:

Your task is to modify the Lambda function `VOCTranscribeFunction`, to handle the "Start Transcription" button action. 

- Refer to the [AWS SDK](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-javascript/v3/developer-guide/transcribe-examples-section.html#transcribe-start-transcription) sample code to fix the function. You need to call the method `StartTranscriptionJobCommand` to process a pre-recorded audio file.

The lab has been provisioned with the following resources: 
- React Application -- VoC application frontend to process customer complaint.
- Amazon S3 -- All your audio files are hosted here.
- Amazon API Gateway -- supply backend to web based UI application. 
- Amazon Lambda Function -- `VOCTranscribeFunction` you will be interacting with.
- Amazon Bedrock -- Large Language Model (LLM) you will be using.

- AWS Lambda Functions

## Task Validation:

If successful, you should see the transcribed script based on the Audio file input in the VoC Application UI.

------------
## Reference
The VoC WebUI contains a pre-recorded audio file and few buttons:

- **Play** button - you can listen to the feedback content in English.
- **Start Transcription** button - to call the backend API and invoke the `VOCTranscribeFunction`.
- **Check Status** button  - to monitor the transcription progress. Upon completion, the transcript will appear within 2 minutes.
- **Summarize** buton - Once the transcribed script is available, hit the button to generate the summary based on the VoC input. Behind the scene, it interacts with a Lambda function triggering a GenAI model from Bedrock.

challengeTitle: Unlocking Insights: Understanding the Voice of the Customer
content:
### Background: 

In Task 1, you successfully transcribed customer interactions. However, the speech-to-text output is not in a format that is easily understood by your end user - customer relationship manager.
To resolve this, you will use a Large Language Model (LLM) in Amazon Bedrock to translate and summarize the customer feedback in English, following this structure:
- **Product**: Product description (max 10 words).
- **Caller**: Customer's name (max 10 words).
- **Key topics**: Complaint summary (max 50 words).

Example:

```json
* Product: Lego set
* Caller: Chen
* Key topics: Missing a bag of components in the Lego set, request for re-send.
```
----

### Getting Started: 

1. Enable Model access in Bedrock:
   - **Go to the AWS Management Console** and navigate to **Amazon Bedrock**.
   - Locate **Access Model** from the side menu.
   - Enable the model **Mistral Large (24.02)**.
2. Update a Bedrock Lambda function:
	- Navigate to **Lambda Function** in AWS, select `VocBedrockIntegrationFunction`, and open `index.js` file
	- Find `CHANGE HERE` to identify where prompt engineer is required.
----

### Your Task:
In the VoC WebUI, the `[Translate and Summarise]` button is not currently producing summarized insights. Your task is to integrate the LLM to translate the transcription and generate a structured summary for the CRMs.
* Modify the `prompt` variable in the `VocBedrockIntegrationFunction` Lambda function 
* The prompt should instruct the LLM to translate and summarize the customer feedback into English, following the format you specified in the prompt.

## Inventory:
The lab has been provisioned with the following resources: 
- React Application -- VoC application frontend to process customer complaint.
- Amazon S3 -- All your audio files are hosted here.
- Amazon API Gateway -- supply backend to web based UI application. 
- Amazon Lambda Function -- `VOCTranscribeFunction` you will be interacting with.
- Amazon Bedrock -- Large Language Model (LLM) you will be using.

## Services You Should Use:
- Amazon Bedrock
- AWS Lambda

## Task Validation:
The task is complete when the LLM generates formatted English summaries, which will be displayed on the VoC application.

---
## Reference:
- Document to craft an [effective prompt](https://docs.mistral.ai/guides/prompting_capabilities/)
- To construct your prompt in this task, consider these tips:
	* **Unambiguous prompts** - for example: "Output your evaluation result to include 'Product', 'Caller' and 'Key topics' fields."
	* **Communicate clearly** - for example: "Convert the customer complaint conversation into English."
	* **Provide context** - for example: "This is for visualisation."
	* **Targeting Your Questions** - for example: "Carefully review the provided transcription."

content:
## Background

You're a security consultant and you've been tasked to review security posture of a new application that your customer has deployed. The CISO is concerned that developers are taking security shortcuts and leaving vulnerabilities in the application and possibly even purposely leaking sensitive data. The security team has heard several rumors and they'd like you to see if there's any truth to them.
## Your Task

**The latest rumor:** One of the developers doesn't want to remember the administration password for the application. Thinking he was being clever, he hid it somewhere "in plain sight" in the application so he can retrieve it with just his desktop Web browser and use it to derive the password. Your task is to follow up on this rumor and see if there's data hidden somewhere easily accessible to the public that can be used to derive the password.

## Getting Started

- The application has been deployed on a Web server. You can find the address of the server in the Output Properties for this challenge.
- Visit the Web site with an ordinary browser and find the hidden data that can be used to derive the password.
- Remember, the CISO assumes that you have experience with basic security, encryption, and binary encoding concepts and have access to the appropriate tools to complete the task.

## Inventory
- A single Web server hosting the application. Its address is in output properties.

## Services You Should Use
- No additional AWS services are required or available to complete this task.
- You should use your own or public Web-based security and analysis tools.

## Task Validation
Once you have found the data and derived the password, enter the password in the box above and press submit.

challengeTitle: All Roads Lead to Gateway Load Balancer: A Transit Gateway Centralized Inspection Love Story
content:
# Background

Take a close look at the [architecture diagram](https://aws-jam-challenge-resources.s3.amazonaws.com/gwlb-tgw-packet-inspection/GWLB_TGW_FIGURE1.jpg) and consider the fact that your instance in Spoke 1 should be able to reach out to the Internet. What's more - is that all traffic destined for the Internet and its return traffic should be subject to inspection by our Appliances, courtesy of Gateway Load Balancer.

Transit Gateway is a Layer 3 next hop destination for traffic, and we want to send everything but traffic bound for the local VPC CIDR toward the Transit Gateway. In addition, we need to ensure that once traffic reaches the Transit Gateway, it is then subject to inspection by our Appliance fleet - both in the egress and ingress directions.

Let's start out by implementing the **VPC Route Table** modifications that permit this.

# Your Task

Your specific task for this stage is to implement the VPC Route Table modifications in Spoke 1 VPC and the Appliance VPC
to provide for North-South connectivity from an instance in AZ-a in Spoke 1 VPC through to the Internet and back. 

# Getting Started

Referring to the diagram, we can see we have our **Egress** Transit Gateway Route Table, providing an egress route for the Internet traffic through the Appliance fleet. You need to make sure
that traffic from the Spoke 1 VPC subnet containing our application instances has a bidirectional path via the Transit Gateway, Appliance Fleet (via the Gateway Load Balancer) and the NAT Gateway.

Look closely at each of these hops in the traffic flow to ensure North-South connectivity is intact!

# Inventory

* Application-1a instance in Spoke 1 VPC
* Appliance instances in Appliance VPC
* Gateway Load Balancer Endpoints (GWLBe) in each AZ of the Appliance VPC
* NAT Gateways in each AZ of the Appliance VPC
* Internet Gateway attached to the Appliance VPC

# Services You Should Use

In order to accomplish this task effectively, you should use the following services:

* Session Manager launched from EC2 console to Application-1a instance
* VPC Route Tables of Spoke 1 VPC
* VPC Route Tables of Appliance VPC

# Task Validation

The task will be automatically complete once you find the solution. In addition you can always check your 
progress by pressing the “Check my progress” Button in the challenge details screen. From the Application-1a instance in Spoke 1 VPC you should be able
to ping an Internet destination, with the command `ping amazon.com`.

challengeTitle: All Roads Lead to Gateway Load Balancer: A Transit Gateway Centralized Inspection Love Story
content:
# Background In Transit Gateway-based architectures, it is common to subject both North-South _and_ East-West traffic to inspection by things like AWS Network Firewall, Gateway Load Balancers + fleets of Appliances, and more. In Task 1, we enabled North-South connectivity by adding select VPC Route Table entries. In this task, we will make sure an instance in Spoke 1 AZ-a can ping an instance in Spoke 2 AZ-a. # Your Task In this task, we want to accomplish East-West connectivity between two Application instances in AZ-a of the Spoke 1 and 2 VPCs through the Transit Gateway. When in doubt, look closely at the [architecture diagram](https://aws-jam-challenge-resources.s3.amazonaws.com/gwlb-tgw-packet-inspection/GWLB_TGW_FIGURE1.jpg)! # Getting Started Using Session Manager initiated in the EC2 console, connect to the Application-1a instance. Try and ping the Application-2a instance with 
ping 10.0.1.40
Does it get through? Do you see a reply? Probably not; bummer. Let's fix it! Both of the subnets that contain our Application instances in both Spoke 1 and 2 VPCs ought to have their default route pointing toward Transit Gateway. And, our Security Groups are allowing all traffic to and from the CIDRs of each VPC. So then, what else could be wrong? We know from Task 1 that all Spoke 1 VPC traffic except the local CIDR is going through the Appliance fleet. Now, think about how you can make the traffic from Spoke 1 VPC and destined for Spoke 2 VPC via a "detour" through the Appliance Fleet. # Inventory * Application instances in Spoke 1 and 2 VPCs, in AZ-a * Transit Gateway Route Table entitled "Transit Route Table" * Transit Gateway attachments already in place for all VPCs * VPC Route Tables # Services You Should Use In order to accomplish this task, you should use the following services: * Session Manager launched from EC2 console to Application-1a instance * Transit Gateway Route Tables * VPC Route Tables # Task Validation The task will be automatically complete once you find the solution. In addition you can always check your progress by pressing the “Check my progress” Button in the challenge details screen. But, you will know you are done with this Task when you can successfully ping the Application instance at 10.0.1.40 and receive replies. **_Note_**: Any Transit Gateway routes inputted for this task should be _propagated_, not _statically inputted_.

challengeTitle: All Roads Lead to Gateway Load Balancer: A Transit Gateway Centralized Inspection Love Story
content:
# Background ##### Read Me First! In Transit Gateway architectures that involve multiple AZs (as all well-architected infrastructures should!) we have a _slight_ problem with the logic of Transit Gateway's out-of-the-box functionality when communicating across AZs - such as while communicating from Application-1a instance of Spoke 1 VPC to the Application-1b instance of Spoke 2 VPC. You see, Transit Gateway attempts to minimize latency and cross-AZ charges for our customers by keeping traffic in the same AZ from which it originated, whenever possible. This means traffic from Application-1a instance will go to Transit Gateway ENI in AZ-a of Appliance VPC. This traffic will then go to the Gateway Load Balancer Endpoint in the same AZ i.e. AZ-a. This works fine for intra AZ communication between the Spokes. However, the inter-AZ communication breaks because of this behavior. Consider Application-1a Instance is talking to Application-2b Instance. Think about the return traffic, which is coming from Application-2b instance of Spoke-2 VPC. This traffic will hit the transit gateway ENI in AZ-b and hence the Gateway Load Balancer ENI in AZ-b. Since the forward traffic (from Application-1a instance), went to Gateway Load Balancer Endpoint in AZ-a, this causes asymmetric routing. Gateway Load Balancer ENI in AZ-b, being unaware of the flow for the return traffic, will drop the return traffic. # Your Task Your challenge on this Task is to leverage a cool feature of Transit Gateway, which allows for Traffic to cross-AZs such that both forward and return traffic hits the same AZ's Transit Gateway ENI. This ensures that the traffic in both directions is traversing the same Gateway Load Balancer Endpoint. # Getting Started From your Application-1a instance, which you can reach via Session Manager initiated in the EC2 console, try to ping the Application-2b instance, with: 
ping 10.0.1.10
Do you see a reply to that ping? It's strange - everything seems to be in place for this to work - Transit Gateway Route Tables are there, Security Groups look good, VPC Route Tables are all sending traffic to the TGW - we were even able to ping the Application-2a instance - why not Application-2b? ### Curiouser and Curiouser Let's start out by describing the Transit Gateway VPC Attachments. From your Application-1a instance in Session Manager, try running the command: 
aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-vpc-attachments
You should get back your three TGW attachments. Do you see the **options** field? Which option do you think will prevent the asymmetric routing? See below for an example block of the output of this command: 
           
"Options": {
                "DnsSupport": "enable",
                "Ipv6Support": "disable",
                "ApplianceModeSupport": "disable"
            }
These three flags look interesting; try researching a little on appliances deployed in this manner to determine the right course of action to take from here on. You're almost there! # Inventory * Application instance in Spoke 1 VPC * AWS CLI v2 # Services You Should Use * Session Manager initiated from EC2 console to Application A instance in Spoke 1 VPC. * AWS VPC Console, Transit Gateway Attachments # Task Validation The task will be automatically complete once you find the solution. In addition you can always check your progress by pressing the “Check my progress” Button in the challenge details screen. But, you will know you have completed this task if you successfully receive replies back to your pings to 10.0.1.10 from your Application-1a instance (**Note**: you may have to wait up to 2 minutes after applying your change to see replies).

***Note: This challenge requires 3-5min additional wait time before attempting to connect with RDP to Ubuntu Desktop, to verify the challenge readiness -> login into the console, verify in Amazon ECR if the image nginx-webapp:latest exists. For extensive connection issues, restart the challenge or communicate with event facilitator.*** **Background:** The Terraform Model Context Protocol (MCP) server enhances AI models with real-time access to current Terraform provider documentation, modules, and policies from the Terraform registry. This ensures AI-generated Terraform configurations use accurate, up-to-date information rather than potentially outdated training data. In this workshop, we will be using Kiro IDE, an AI-powered development environment specifically designed for building AI agents. **Your Task:** Deploy the Terraform MCP Server using Docker and configure it globally in the Kiro IDE. **Prerequisites:** 1. Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) for Mac / Windows or similar alternative installed on the participant device locally. 2. Read through the steps to setup Kiro IDE in the Ubuntu Desktop 3. Create account in AWS Builder ID 3. Log in to the AWS Console. **Inventory:** In order to get to the hands-on-keyboard portion of the workshop as quickly as possible, we have provisioned an Ubuntu Desktop hosted on an Amazon EC2 Instance with all required software which you can access via Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). Open the `Output Properties` in the JAM Console, here you have available the connection details for the Ubuntu instance: - `InstanceId`: Ubuntu Desktop instance for Kiro Setup - `RDPAddress`: The address you'll use to connect to your instance - `RDPUsername`: The username for logging in - `RDPPassword`: The password for logging in (copy this for later use) Use the information from `RDPConnectionInfo` to guide you through the RDP connection process. ***Note:*** For connection use `RDPAddress:3389` **Getting Started:** 1. Verify in Amazon ECR, that the image `nginx-webapp:latest` exists, before attempting RDP connect. 2. Open Amazon EC2 service, find the Ubuntu Desktop with `InstanceId`, modify the security group inbound rule to "My IP". 3. Use `Prerequsites #2` link for guidance to setup Kiro IDE via Remote Desktop. ***Important Note!*** Follow all the steps in the Kiro guidance till the end, including "First Run Setup" 3. Get used to the interface of Kiro IDE: - Setup as current project "Desktop" - Open the terminal in IDE - Run the command in terminal to verify that Terraform is installed `terraform --version`, `docker --version` - Experiment with the vibe coding feature of Kiro with simple prompts `"I want to setup a simple terraform project in us-east-1 region, help me with the basic setup, no resources."` 3. Setup Terraform MCP Server via docker with Kiro as AI client. Docker provides the most reliable and consistent way to run the Terraform MCP server across different environments. 4. Modify your user settings JSON file, for the MCP configuration to be global. **Services You Should Use:** - Amazon EC2 - Security Groups - Kiro IDE - Terraform CLI - Google Chrome to access AWS Builder ID **Task Validation:** 1. Get Access to Kiro IDE from inside the EC2 via RDP, login to Kiro with one of the `AWS Builder ID` sign-in option. 2. Terraform MCP server is connected via docker and recognized by Kiro. 3. When you are ready to validate the configuration, click on the challenge button "Check my progress".

taskTitle: Create your static website in S3
content:
Background

Your product is taking off and you need to set up a static website ASAP.

Services You Should Use

S3

Your Tasks

Here are your steps to say Hello to the World using AWS:

1) Create a bucket (only create one). Your bucket name must start with "aws-jam-" (e.g., aws-jam-mywebsite-123)

2) Enable static website hosting on your bucket

3) Enable public access to your bucket by editing the "Block Public Access" settings

4) Add a bucket policy that makes your bucket content publicly available. Here is the policy to use:
{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Sid": "PublicReadGetObject",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Principal": "*",
            "Action": [ "s3:GetObject" ],
"Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::Bucket-Name/*" ]
        }
    ]
}

5) Create an index.html file and upload it to your bucket.
Here is an HTML example to use:



   


   

Hello AWS Jam!


   

Now hosted on Amazon S3!



6) Create an upload an error file using the same file name when you configured static hosting on your bucket.
Here is an HTML example to use:



   


   

You have an Error :(


   

UGH!



7) Test your Jam's endpoint and save that endpoint for Jam Submission in the next step.
At the bottom of the Properties tab of your bucket, you can find your Bucket's website endpoint.

Task Validation

In the "task section" on the challenge builder menu, you can paste the URL of your S3 bucket into the text box and an automated script will check to see if the challenge is complete.

you can find the resource names from "Output Properties" of the challenge dashboard.

challengeTitle: Build HIPAA-compliant AI with automated data discovery
content:
Background:
Medcorp stores sensitive medical records across multiple S3 buckets. As the newly appointed AI Engineer, your first task is to implement automated PHI discovery and classification using Amazon Macie with custom healthcare-specific identifiers. The data contains Patient IDs, Clinical Trial IDs, and Provider Numbers that need to be identified and protected.

Getting Started:
1. Navigate to the Amazon Macie console
2. Review the provided medical datasets in S3 buckets:
   - medcorp-clinical-notes-${AWS::AccountId}
   - medcorp-research-data-${AWS::AccountId}
   - medcorp-insurance-claims-${AWS::AccountId}
3. Familiarize yourself with Amazon Macie documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/macie/latest/user/what-is-macie.html

Inventory:
- Three S3 buckets with different types of medical data:
  - Clinical Notes bucket: Contains patient visit records
  - Research Data bucket: Contains clinical trial data
  - Insurance Claims bucket: Contains billing records
- Custom data identifier templates
- Macie findings destination bucket

Services You Should Use:
- Amazon Macie
- AWS KMS
- Amazon S3

Your Task:
1. Enable Amazon Macie for your account
2. Create custom data identifiers for healthcare-specific patterns:
   - Patient IDs (Pattern: PAT-\d{6}-[A-Z]{2})
   - Clinical Trial IDs (Pattern: CT-\d{4}-[A-Z]{3})
   - Provider Numbers (Pattern: PRV-[A-Z]{2}\d{4})
3. Configure classification jobs for all three buckets
4. Set up findings export with encryption using AWS KMS

Task Validation:
The validation Lambda will verify:
- Macie is enabled
- All required custom data identifiers are created
- Classification jobs are running on all buckets
- Findings export is properly configured

The validation will pass when all components are correctly set up and the classification job is in an active state.

content:
Title: Implement Dynamic AI Protection with Bedrock Guardrails

Background: 
MedCorp wants to leverage AI models for medical research and analysis but needs to ensure PHI is protected during AI interactions. Your task is to set up Amazon Bedrock Guardrails that dynamically adapt based on Macie findings to prevent exposure of sensitive data.

Architecture Overview:
```
┌─────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐
│   Clinical      │    │   Research       │    │   Insurance     │
│   Notes S3      │    │   Data S3        │    │   Claims S3     │
│   Bucket        │    │   Bucket         │    │   Bucket        │
└─────────┬───────┘    └─────────┬────────┘    └─────────┬───────┘
          │                      │                       │
          └──────────────────────┼───────────────────────┘
                                 │
                    ┌────────────▼────────────┐
                    │      Amazon Macie       │
                    │   (PHI Discovery &      │
                    │   Classification)       │
                    └────────────┬────────────┘
                                 │
                                 │ Findings Export
                                 ▼
                    ┌────────────────────────────┐
                    │    Macie Findings S3       │
                    │    (.jsonl.gz files)       │
                    └────────────┬───────────────┘
                                 │
                                 │ S3 Event
                                 ▼
                    ┌────────────────────────────┐
                    │     Amazon EventBridge     │
                    │      (S3 Event Rule)       │
                    └────────────┬───────────────┘
                                 │
                                 │ Trigger
                                 ▼
                    ┌────────────────────────────┐
                    │   DynamicGuardrail Lambda  │
                    │   1. Parse Macie findings  │
                    │   2. Extract PHI patterns  │
                    │   3. Generate regex rules  │
                    └────────────┬───────────────┘
                                 │
                                 │ Update
                                 ▼
                    ┌────────────────────────────┐
                    │    Amazon Bedrock          │
                    │    Guardrail Service       │
                    │   (Block PHI in AI)        │
                    └────────────────────────────┘
```

Getting Started:
• Review the Bedrock Guardrails documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html
• Examine the Macie findings from Task 1 in the designated S3 bucket
• Familiarize yourself with the Bedrock API and available foundation models

Inventory:
• Macie findings bucket from Task 1
• Bedrock foundation models: Nova
• Lambda function template for dynamic guardrail updates
• Sample medical research queries

Services You Should Use:
• Amazon Bedrock
• AWS Lambda
• Amazon S3
• Amazon EventBridge

Your Task:
1. Create a base Bedrock Guardrail configuration that blocks known PHI patterns.

2. Fix the Incomplete Lambda Function: The `DynamicGuardrailLambda` function has several issues that need to be fixed:
   • Reads new Macie findings from the S3 bucket
   • Updates Bedrock Guardrails dynamically based on newly discovered sensitive data patterns

3. Set up an EventBridge rule to trigger the Lambda function when new Macie findings are generated.

4. Configure Bedrock to use the guardrails for Nova models.

5. Test the system with newly generated Macie findings.

Task Validation: 
The validation Lambda will check:
• Bedrock Guardrails are properly configured
• Lambda function correctly processes Macie findings
• EventBridge rule is set up to trigger the Lambda
• Sample queries do not return PHI when submitted to Bedrock models

content:
### Background
Great job! You have successfully migrated your data from the on-premises NFS server to Amazon S3 using AWS DataSync. Now it's time to provide seamless access to this migrated data through AWS Storage Gateway - S3 File Gateway.

AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway enables you to store and retrieve objects in Amazon S3 using file protocols such as NFS. Refer to this doc: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/filegateway/latest/files3/what-is-file-s3.html

In this task, you will activate the Storage Gateway instance that has been pre-deployed for you and configure it. 

![s3upload](https://aws-jam-challenge-resources.s3.amazonaws.com/hybrid-storage-setup/JAM-Bytes-2.png)

### Your Task
1. Allow connection from your own device's ip address to the File Gateway Instance on port 80.

challengeTitle: Investigate Hidden S3 Access and Rotate Aged IAM Keys
content:
## Background

Your organization's security team has discovered that IAM user `legacy-backup-user` has access keys that are 120 days old. The AWS Cost and Usage Report shows Amazon S3 API charges for this user, but when you search AWS CloudTrail for Amazon S3 events from this user, you find nothing. This discrepancy has raised serious security concerns.

How can there be Amazon S3 activity generating costs without corresponding AWS CloudTrail events? The answer lies in understanding the difference between **management events** and **data events** in AWS CloudTrail.

The mystery of missing Amazon S3 events in AWS CloudTrail is a common security blind spot. By default, AWS CloudTrail only captures management events, which include operations like creating buckets, modifying bucket policies, or managing access control lists. However, the actual data operations such as uploading files, downloading objects, or deleting content are considered **data events** and require special configuration.

Think about the difference between managing a filing cabinet versus actually putting files in or taking files out of it. AWS CloudTrail treats these as completely different types of activities. The `legacy-backup-user` might be actively accessing files in Amazon S3 buckets, but these operations remain invisible in your current logging configuration.

## Your Task

Investigate and uncover the hidden Amazon S3 activity by configuring proper logging in AWS CloudTrail. You need to enable the right type of event logging to capture what operations the `legacy-backup-user` has been performing on Amazon S3 resources.

To solve this mystery, you need to create a NEW AWS CloudTrail trail specifically configured to capture Amazon S3 data events. This will reveal all the object-level operations that have been happening behind the scenes.

## Inventory

### Services You Should Use:
- [AWS CloudTrail](https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail/)
- [Amazon S3](https://console.aws.amazon.com/s3/)
- [AWS IAM](https://console.aws.amazon.com/iam/)

### Current Resources:
- IAM user: `legacy-backup-user` with 120-day-old access keys
- Existing S3 buckets with hidden activity
- Current CloudTrail trails (management events only)

## Getting Started

1. **Review the current AWS CloudTrail configuration** to understand what's missing
2. Create a NEW AWS CloudTrail trail (do not modify existing trails)
3. Name your new trail starting with `"jam-s3-investigation"`
4. Do **NOT** enable KMS encryption when creating the trail
5. Configure Amazon S3 data events for all current and future buckets

## Links to follow

Please go through the below documents before proceeding with the task.

[+] Understanding CloudTrail events : https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-events.html

[+] What are the differences between data events and management events in CloudTrail? : https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/cloudtrail-data-management-events

[+] Creating a trail with the CloudTrail console: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-create-a-trail-using-the-console-first-time.html

## Task Validation

Your solution will be automatically validated based on proper AWS CloudTrail data events configuration for Amazon S3 operations.

taskTitle: Create Amazon Athena Table and Discover Amazon S3 Events
content:
## Background

Now that AWS CloudTrail is capturing Amazon S3 data events, you need to analyze these logs to understand exactly what the `legacy-backup-user` has been doing. The logs are stored in Amazon S3 as JSON files, but querying them directly would be impractical. Amazon Athena provides a powerful way to create a queryable table structure over these log files.

AWS CloudTrail logs contain a wealth of information, but they're stored as compressed JSON files in Amazon S3. To effectively analyze this data, you need to create a structured table in Amazon Athena that can parse and query these logs.

Amazon Athena uses a **schema-on-read** approach, meaning you define the table structure that maps to the JSON fields in your AWS CloudTrail logs. Once the table is created, you can use standard SQL queries to search for specific users, time ranges, and event types.

## Your Task

Create an Amazon Athena table from your AWS CloudTrail logs and run queries to identify the specific Amazon S3 operations performed by `legacy-backup-user`. You need to discover evidence of the hidden activity that's been generating costs.

The key to solving this challenge is understanding that the `legacy-backup-user`'s Amazon S3 operations will now appear in your data events logs. You need to query for this specific user and look for Amazon S3 object-level operations in the results.

## Inventory

### Services You Should Use:
- [AWS CloudTrail](https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail/)
- [Amazon Athena](https://console.aws.amazon.com/athena/)
- [Amazon S3](https://console.aws.amazon.com/s3/)
- [AWS IAM](https://console.aws.amazon.com/iam/)

### Required Resources:
- CloudTrail trail starting with `"jam-s3-investigation"` (from Task 1)
- S3 bucket for CloudTrail logs starting with `"jam-s3-investigation"`
- **Athena query results bucket:** `aws-athena-query-results--`
- IAM user: `legacy-backup-user`

## Getting Started

1. **Use the AWS CloudTrail console to create an Amazon Athena table** and select the Amazon S3 bucket where your new trail stores logs
2. Table name must start with `"jam-s3-investigation"`
3. Configure Amazon Athena query result location before running queries
4. **Build and run SQL queries** to discover `legacy-backup-user` activities:
   - Query for specific username in `useridentity.username` field
   - Filter for S3 event names like `GetObject`, `PutObject`, `DeleteObject`
   - Example pattern: `SELECT * FROM table_name WHERE useridentity.username = 'legacy-backup-user'`
5. Query for `legacy-backup-user` activities to discover Amazon S3 operations

**Important** - It may take 5-10 minutes for new logs to appear in query results

## Links to follow

Please go through the below documents before proceeding with the task.

[+] Use the CloudTrail console to create an Athena table for CloudTrail logs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/create-cloudtrail-table-ct.html

[+] Specify a query result location : https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/query-results-specify-location.html

[+] Run SQL queries in Amazon Athena : https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/querying-athena-tables.html

## Task Validation

Your solution will be automatically validated based on:
1. **Successful Amazon Athena table creation** with proper CloudTrail log mapping
2. **Athena query results bucket configuration** for storing query outputs
3. **Running queries and discovering Amazon S3 events** in query results showing `legacy-backup-user` activity

taskTitle: Safely Rotate Aged IAM Access Keys
content:
## Background

After discovering the hidden Amazon S3 activity patterns, you now understand how the `legacy-backup-user` has been accessing resources. However, the aged access keys represent a significant security risk and must be rotated immediately. The challenge is performing this rotation without breaking any systems that might be using these keys.

AWS IAM access key rotation is a critical security practice, but it must be done carefully to avoid breaking applications or services that depend on those keys. The safest approach is to create new keys first, test them thoroughly, and only then deactivate the old keys.

The `legacy-backup-user` likely has automated processes or applications using the current access keys for Amazon S3 operations. A poorly executed rotation could cause these processes to fail, potentially impacting business operations.

## Your Task

Perform a safe, zero-downtime rotation of the aged IAM access keys while ensuring continuous service availability. You must follow proper security procedures to avoid service disruption.

Your rotation strategy must include creating new credentials, testing their functionality with actual Amazon S3 operations, and then safely transitioning from old to new keys. The validation system will check that you've successfully created new keys and that they're being actively used.

## Inventory

### Services You Should Use:
- [AWS IAM](https://console.aws.amazon.com/iam/)
- [AWS CloudTrail](https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail/) (for monitoring key usage)
- [Amazon S3](https://console.aws.amazon.com/s3/) (for testing new keys)
- AWS CLI (for key testing)

### Required Resources:
- IAM user: `legacy-backup-user` with existing aged access keys
- S3 buckets for testing new key functionality
- Local terminal/command line interface with AWS CLI installed
- CloudTrail logs to verify key usage patterns

## Getting Started

1. **Do NOT delete old access keys immediately** - maintain service continuity
2. **Create new access keys before deactivating old ones** - follow safe rotation practices
3. **Test new keys comprehensively** with multiple Amazon S3 operations:
   - Verify authentication with `aws sts get-caller-identity`
   - Test S3 bucket listing with `aws s3 ls`
   - Test specific bucket access with `aws s3 ls s3://bucket-name`
   - Validate API operations with `aws s3api list-buckets`
4. **Monitor AWS CloudTrail for key usage patterns** to ensure new keys are working
5. **Verify new keys work with AWS CLI commands** before deactivating old keys

**Important** - Wait 5-10 minutes for CloudTrail to show the new key usage in "Last used" field

## Links to follow

Please go through the below documents before proceeding with the task.

[+] Manage access keys for IAM users: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_access-keys.html

[+] Authenticating using IAM user credentials for the AWS CLI : https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/v1/userguide/cli-authentication-user.html

[+] s3 CLI Commands : https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3/

## Task Validation

Your solution will be automatically validated based on:
1. **Successful creation of new access keys** for `legacy-backup-user`
2. **Proper testing of functionality** including successful S3 operations using new keys with evidence in CloudTrail logs
3. **Safe deactivation of old keys** without service disruption while maintaining exactly one active key

challengeTitle: Lost in Metadata: Solving the EC2 Instance Puzzle
content:
#### Background
---
Amazon EC2 **Instance metadata** is data about your instance that you can use to configure or manage the running instance. You can access EC2 instance metadata from inside of the instance itself or from the EC2 console, API, SDKs, or the AWS CLI. There are different AWS agents like **Amazon SSM** agent, **Amazon CloudWatch** agent, **AWS CLI**, etc. who query instance metadata to retrieve instance related details for their functioning.

To access instance metadata properties from within a running instance, you get the data from the following IPv4 or IPv6 URIs. These IP addresses are link-local addresses and are valid only from the instance. 

- **IPv4** - `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`
- **IPv6** - `http://[fd00:ec2::254]/latest/meta-data/`

The route to instance metadata is by default added in the Windows route table as can be seen in the following screenshot:

![windows-routes](https://aws-jam-challenge-resources.s3.amazonaws.com/inaccessible-metadata/windows-routes.png)

This route is added with Gateway IP of the configured VPC subnet however when the AMI (Amazon Machine Image) of an EC2 Windows instance is captured without **Sysprep** then this captured Gateway IP route in the image doesn't get updated when a new EC2 instance is launched in different VPC subnet and ultimately leads to invalid route issue. With this incorrect route existing in the Windows route table, the instance metadata becomes inaccessible to the instance, causing it to throw following error, halting operations of all dependent AWS agents and other:

`Waiting for the metadata service.....` 

So in this challenge task, since the AMIs (Amazon Machine Images) for EC2 instances are captured from a different AWS account VPC and now being launched in another VPC subnet may have possibly seen similar conflict for invalid Gateway IP address.

To investigate this ahead, you're required to connect one of the given EC2 instance however you found that the EC2 instance is not accessible via Remote Desktop Connection (RDP). To access the instance from your source location, you require to configure the network settings which will enable RDP as well as allow Internet access to the given EC2 instance.

You must check the attached Security Group to the given **Production-Server** instance if it allows RDP and Internet traffic in its defined inbound and outbound rule. 
#### Your Task
---
Your task is to:

* Identify the **Production-Server** EC2 Windows instance
* Enable RDP and Internet access from the instance's Security Group
* Connect the EC2 instance via RDP

#### Getting Started
---
* **Identify the EC2 instance** - From the EC2 Management Console, identify the **Production-Server** EC2 instance by referring to the Instance ID provided in the **Output Properties** section. 

* **Enable RDP and Internet Access** - Please ensure that RDP access to the EC2 instance is allowed from your source network by having the concerned inbound rule added in the associated Security group (specify **Source** as **"My IP"**). Additionally, check if the Internet traffic is allowed in the outbound rule of the same Security Group.

* **Locate the public IP address of the EC2 instance** - Find the **Public IPv4 address** from the EC2 instance details tab.

* **Connect to the EC2 instance via RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) Connection** - After enabling RDP and Internet access, connect to the EC2 Windows instance via RDP client from your source Windows machine (for macOS download the Windows App (formerly Microsoft Remote Desktop) from the AppStore). Open RDP client and enter the public IPv4 address. When prompted, log in using the following **RDP Login Credentials:**

> - **Username:** `Administrator`
> - **Password:** `p@SSword@123`
>
> These credentials are pre-configured for you to use and are also available in the **Output Properties** section. No need to worry about retrieving or decrypting the password from the EC2 console — the credentials above are all you need to connect.

#### Inventory
---
* Amazon EC2 Instance (Windows) named **Production-Server**.
* Security Group attached to the EC2 instance named **Production-SecurityGroup**.

## Background
MedBridge's doctors are in crisis mode! They write detailed medical reports using precise clinical terminology, but patients panic when they read them. Last week, a patient saw "bilateral pneumothorax with subcutaneous emphysema" and immediately called their lawyer to draft a will. Another patient with "benign paroxysmal positional vertigo" rushed to the emergency room thinking they were having a stroke. The misunderstandings are causing chaos!

The Chief Medical Officer is demanding immediate action: "We have this brilliant knowledge base with all our medical communication guidelines, but it's useless without an intelligent system to apply them! We need an AI agent that automatically transforms these terrifying medical reports into something patients can actually understand. No more 3 AM panic calls from patients googling their diagnoses!"

## Your Task

Create and deploy an AI-powered Bedrock Agent that acts as an intelligent medical interpreter, automatically transforming intimidating clinical reports into compassionate, easy-to-understand patient explanations. This agent will leverage your auto-syncing medical knowledge base to identify complex medical terminology and replace it with patient-friendly language. You'll configure the agent with specialized instructions that ensure every medical report becomes accessible while maintaining accuracy, turning technical documentation into clear communication that reduces patient anxiety and improves health outcomes.

## Getting Started

1. Time to build your medical interpreter! Navigate to the Bedrock Agent console and create a new agent with the name report-enhancer-agent, select Amazon Nova Lite as the foundation model, and use the existing medical-agent-service-role-jam role for permissions.

2. The agent needs expert medical communication instructions. Download and copy the complete instructions from [medical-agent-instructions.txt](https://aws-jam-challenge-resources.s3.amazonaws.com/intelligent-content-transform/medical-agent-instructions.txt) into the Instructions field.

3. Save the agent configuration first to establish the foundation before adding knowledge capabilities.

4. Now connect the agent's brain! Attach your medical-kb knowledge base and provide clear instructions about its purpose: "This medical knowledge brain contains comprehensive guidelines for translating complex medical terminology into patient-friendly language."

5. Prepare the agent for deployment, ensuring all configurations are properly saved and the agent is ready to transform medical reports.

## Background

MedBridge's audio report system just triggered a major patient safety incident! A routine pathology report containing the phrase "no evidence of fatal complications" was converted to audio. When the elderly patient heard the word "fatal," they became so distressed they required emergency sedation. Another case involved a psychiatric evaluation mentioning "suicide risk factors" in the audio summary, causing a recovering patient to relapse into severe anxiety.

The Compliance Officer is demanding immediate action: "These sensitive medical terms are necessary in clinical documentation, but they're causing real harm when patients hear them in audio format. Some words simply shouldn't be spoken aloud to vulnerable patients. We need automatic filtering before another patient gets hurt!"

## Your Task

Build a robust safety system using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails that acts as an intelligent content filter, automatically detecting and blocking potentially harmful or distressing medical terminology before audio conversion. You'll configure comprehensive word filters to catch sensitive terms like "fatal," "suicide," and "abuse," create appropriate messaging for blocked content, integrate these guardrails with your medical report agent, and deploy a production-ready alias. This protective layer ensures patients receive compassionate, safe audio communications while maintaining medical accuracy and preventing psychological harm.

**Reference Documentation:** For detailed guidance on Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, refer to the [AWS Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html). 

## Getting Started

1. The Bedrock console houses a powerful Guardrails feature. Locate this section and initiate creation of your safety filtering system.

2. Your guardrail needs a clear identity. Name it medical-safety-filter and provide a description that explains its role in protecting patients from distressing content.

3. Blocked content requires compassionate handling. Set the blocked message to: *"I apologize, but this medical report contains content that violates our patient safety and content policy guidelines. Please review the report with your healthcare provider for appropriate discussion of sensitive medical information."* Apply this same message for both prompts and responses.

4. Certain words trigger immediate distress when heard aloud. Configure custom word filtering by manually adding these critical terms: "abuse," "fatal," and "suicide" to prevent them from reaching audio conversion.

5. Your report-enhancer-agent currently operates without safety controls. Integrate the medical-safety-filter guardrail to create a protective barrier around all content processing.

6. After adding the guardrail, save and prepare the agent to apply all configurations. This step is critical before creating an alias.

7. Production deployment requires a stable endpoint. Create an alias called report-enhancer-agent-alias that packages your agent with all safety features enabled and ready for patient-facing operations.
   
   **Note:** The alias makes your agent invokable with all configurations (knowledge base + guardrails). You'll need the Alias ID for Task 5. For more information about working with agent aliases, see the [Amazon Bedrock Agent Deployment documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/deploy-agent.html).

I need full automation TODAY - when a doctor uploads a report, patients should receive their audio explanation instantly. No more manual steps, no more delays!"

Complete the automation journey by building an end-to-end serverless pipeline that eliminates all manual intervention in MedBridge's medical report processing. You'll create a sophisticated event-driven architecture where S3 buckets serve as input/output endpoints, Lambda functions orchestrate the workflow, your Bedrock agent transforms complex medical terminology into patient-friendly explanations, and Amazon Polly converts the enhanced text into professional audio narration.
