challengeTitle: Introduction to MapReduce with Apache Spark and Amazon EMR
content:
Before starting the Jam, you will need to setup some resources, which you will do in this task. AWS service names will be introduced and explained briefly here and expanded upon in more detail in the next task. You will be setting up the following resources: * Amazon EMR Cluster * Amazon EMR Studio * Amazon EMR Studio Workspace
# Amazon EMR Cluster Amazon EMR is a big data platform for data processing, petabyte-scale interactive analysis, and machine learning using open source frameworks such as Apache Spark, Apache Hive, and Presto. With EMR you can focus on transforming and analyzing your data without having to worry about managing compute capacity or open-source applications. An Amazon EMR Cluster is a collection of Amazon EC2 instances running big data applications. In order to setup and launch a cluster, follow these steps: * _**Unless otherwise noted, leave the default option as is**_ * On the AWS Management Console, search Amazon EMR * On the EMR Dashboard, click on Clusters under the EMR on EC2 section * Click the Create Cluster button * Name the cluster whatever you want * Click on the Spark Interactive application bundle * In the Cluster Configuration section: * _**IMPORTANT: For Primary EC2 instance type, Core EC2 instance type, and Task EC2 instance type, choose m6i.xlarge.**_ * In the Networking section: * Click on Browse for VPC, choose EMR-Dev-Exp-VPC, and click on the Choose button * Click on Browse for Subnet, choose EMR-Dev-Exp-PublicSubnet1, and click on the Choose button * In the Cluster termination section: * Select Manually terminate cluster * In the Cluster logs section: * Select Publish cluster-specific logs to Amazon S3, click on browse S3, choose the bucket with "emr-dev-exp-xxxxx", and add /logs/ suffix * In the Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles section: * For Amazon EMR Service Role, select "Choose an existing service role" * For Service role, choose "EMRDevExp-EMRClusterServiceRole" * For EC2 instance profile for Amazon EMR, select "Choose an existing user profile" * For Instance profile, choose "EMRDevExp-EMR_EC2_Restricted_Role" * Click on the Create cluster button * Your cluster should be in the process of being created. This can take a few minutes to complete. The cluster will be in waiting state once it completes. * Go ahead and move on to the Studio setup while the Cluster is being made.
# Amazon EMR Studio Amazon EMR Studio is an integrated development environment (IDE) that makes it easy for data scientists and data engineers to develop, visualize, and debug data engineering and data science applications written in R, Python, Scala, and PySpark. It is a fully managed application with single sign-on, fully managed Jupyter Notebooks, automated infrastructure provisioning, and the ability to debug jobs without logging into the AWS Console or cluster. Try to setup EMR Studio on your own, following these general steps: * Go to Amazon EMR Studio dashboard in the Management Console * Create a Studio * It must be a custom Studio * Name the Studio "mapreducejam" * Make sure to also create a Workspace with the Studio * Make sure to use a custom security group * Remember that an Amazon S3 Bucket has already been created for you. Once you get to the Studio Settings section, choose the bucket named “emr-dev-exp-xxxxx” and add the suffix “/workspace”. * A Service role to let Studio access your AWS resources has also already been created for you. Choose the role named “EMRDevExp-EMRStudioServiceRole”. It is imperative that you use the name "mapreducejam" for the Studio. Once successfully created, the Jam platform will check to make sure you have properly created the Studio and label Task 1 as complete. However, _**YOU MUST STILL COMPLETE THE NEXT SECTION: Amazon EMR Studio Workspace.**_
# Amazon EMR Studio Workspace In Amazon EMR Studio, a Workspace is to used to organize and run Jupyter Notebooks. Workspaces are the primary building blocks of Amazon EMR Studio. To organize notebooks, users create one or more Workspaces in a Studio. All notebooks in a Workspace are saved to the same Amazon S3 location and run on the same cluster. Similar to workspaces in JupyterLab, a Workspace preserves the state of notebook work. However, the Workspace user interface extends the open-source JupyterLab interface with additional tools to let you create and attach EMR clusters, run jobs, explore sample notebooks, and link Git repositories. In this Jam, you will mainly be interacting with an EMR Studio Workspace. At this point, you should have successfully set up your Cluster, Studio, and Workspace. The last step is to attach the Workspace to the Cluster so that you can run your jobs. To do this, you will need to perform the following steps: * Once you click on the Create Studio and launch Workspace button from the previous step, the Workspace should open up in a new tab. * Make sure to allow pop-ups in your browser * If the Workspace doesn’t pop-up automatically, go back to the AWS Management Console and Quick Launch a Workspace. * In your Workspace tab: * Attach the Cluster you just created * Select the notebook that you already made and start a PySpark kernel You can now start writing code in the Notebook cells. Continue to the next Task.

challengeTitle: Introduction to MapReduce with Apache Spark and Amazon EMR
content:
# Background
## MapReduce MapReduce, developed by Google in 2004, represents a significant milestone in the evolution of big data processing. This programming model was born out of Google's need to analyze an exponentially growing amount of data generated by their burgeoning search engine. As the internet expanded, Google faced the unprecedented challenge of indexing a vast and rapidly increasing number of web pages, necessitating a robust, scalable, and efficient data processing solution. The power of MapReduce lies in its simplicity and effectiveness in handling large-scale data. The model breaks down tasks into two key phases: the 'Map' phase, where it processes and transforms massive datasets into intermediate key-value pairs, and the 'Reduce' phase, which aggregates these pairs into a more concise set of results. This approach enabled parallel processing across large clusters of computers, significantly speeding up data processing tasks. MapReduce was instrumental in solving Google's indexing problem, allowing them to analyze and process the immense data from the web efficiently. The impact of MapReduce extended far beyond Google’s initial application. It laid the foundation for Apache Hadoop, an open-source framework that brought the power of distributed data processing to a broader audience. Hadoop's adoption across various industries marked a new era in big data analytics, facilitating advancements in areas ranging from genomics to finance. The influence of MapReduce is also evident in the development of subsequent big data technologies and has been integral in furthering fields like machine learning and artificial intelligence by providing a robust backbone for processing large datasets.
## Apache Spark Among those subsequent big data technologies is Apache Spark, an open-source unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing. Apache Spark entered the big data landscape as an evolution of the Apache Hadoop MapReduce implementation, addressing some of its limitations, namely its speed with iterative algorithms and interactive data analysis. Apache Hadoop writes intermediate results to disk, which can be inefficient for complex computations that require multiple MapReduce iterations. Spark was designed to overcome these limitations by utilizing in-memory processing and a generalized MapReduce model known as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Where the normal MapReduce framework has only two steps (Map then Reduce), a DAG generalizes this concept and can have multiple Map and Reduce steps in different orders. This approach allows Spark to perform computations much faster than Hadoop because Spark doesn’t need to read and write from the disk every time it has to interact with the data. Additionally, Spark offers a more flexible and comprehensive data processing framework compared to Hadoop. It supports a variety of workloads like batch processing, real-time streaming, iterative algorithms, and interactive queries, all within the same engine. It is also easier to setup and interact with, hence the use of it in this Jam. The introduction of Spark has had a significant impact on the big data ecosystem. Its ability to process data at unprecedented speeds, coupled with its versatility, has made it a popular choice for data analytics. Spark's integration with other big data tools, various cloud platforms, and its support for multiple programming languages (Scala, Java, Python, and R) have further contributed to its widespread adoption.
## Amazon EMR As an increasing number of companies started realizing the value in analyzing their data, the need for big data processing tools skyrocketed. However, setting up and managing the infrastructure for big data tools such as Hadoop required significant time and technical expertise. AWS recognized this problem and developed Amazon Elastic MapReduce (EMR) in 2009. Amazon EMR was designed to simplify and scale the processing of big data across distributed computing resources. It acts as a managed cluster platform that streamlines the deployment and management of various big data processing frameworks, including Apache Hadoop and Apache Spark. Amazon EMR abstracts much of the complexity of running big data tools on premises, offering a service that automates tasks like cluster provisioning, configuration, and tuning. Users can quickly launch and scale clusters as needed, paying only for the resources they use. Amazon EMR's integration with other AWS services further enhances its utility. It seamlessly integrates with storage services like Amazon S3, database services like DynamoDB, and several others. This integration allows for flexible data storage and retrieval, making it a versatile solution for various big data tasks, from batch processing and streaming to machine learning and scientific simulations. Amazon EMR's introduction marked a pivotal shift in how organizations approach big data processing. It lowered the barrier to entry, enabling businesses of all sizes to leverage powerful big data technologies without the overhead of managing the underlying infrastructure. As a result, Amazon EMR has played a crucial role in democratizing access to big data processing tools, allowing more organizations to harness the power of data for analytics and decision-making.
# Proper Translation to MapReduce Although MapReduce and the technologies based off of it are very powerful tools, it’s important to remember that some problems don’t translate well to the MapReduce framework. Technically, you can translate any problem into a series of Map and Reduce statements, but just because you can doesn’t mean you should. Graph algorithms are notable example of computations that are difficult to efficiently replicate with MapReduce. This is because of things like repeated iterations and data dependencies, which many graph algorithms tend to have. Another well-known challenge for MapReduce based tools is real-time stream processing. There exist add-ons and libraries like Spark Streaming and GraphX, but the use case itself is still challenging for the core engine. Also, the translation to Map and Reduce statements can be time consuming and complicated depending on the problem. Sometimes, it’s better to use different tools or frameworks. Something else to consider is the size of your dataset. For example, if you use Apache Spark to process a small dataset, then you might notice that any performance gains compared to running it on a single machine are negligible. This is because of things like file metadata that has to be created when Spark is processing the input data and task scheduling. Sometimes, preparing a cluster of computers to run a job in parallel takes longer and is more resource intensive than running the actual job.
# Goals In the Summary section of this Jam, you were given context and challenged to answer a question: _Is Player 1 cheating?_ In the following Tasks, you will learn the basics of the MapReduce framework and implement those concepts to answer the question. You will use Amazon EMR and PySpark, the Python API for Apache Spark. Before diving into the details, you need to prepare a Spark Session and load your data. * Initiate a Spark Session * Tip: You don't need a specific function for this. Try "import sys" and run the cell. * Import the games_data.csv file into Spark so that you can start operating on it * Tip: Try spark.read() * Tip: You input the data from S3 using the object URL * Provide an answer to the following problem: How many rows are in the dataset (not including the header)?
# Additional Information * [2003–2023: A Brief History of Big Data](https://towardsdatascience.com/2003-2023-a-brief-history-of-big-data-25712351a6bc) * [MapReduce](https://www.databricks.com/glossary/mapreduce)

# Spark RDDs vs. Spark DataFrames Apache Spark provides two main abstractions for working with data: Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs) and DataFrames. Both are used for distributed data processing, but they have some key differences in terms of abstraction, optimization, and ease of use. ### Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs): * **Lower-Level Abstraction**: RDDs are a low-level abstraction that provides full control over data and transformations. They represent an immutable distributed collection of objects that can be processed in parallel. * **Functional Programming Style**: RDDs are manipulated using functional programming constructs like map, filter, reduce, etc. This requires a good understanding of lambda functions and can be more complex for users not familiar with functional programming. * **Manual Optimization**: With RDDs, developers need to manually optimize their transformations and data shuffling, as there is no in-built optimization engine. * **Use Cases**: RDDs are more suitable for use cases where fine-grained control over data processing is needed, such as custom partitioning of data or when performing complex operations where the higher-level abstractions of DataFrames are not sufficient. ### DataFrames: * **Higher-Level Abstraction**: DataFrames provide a higher-level abstraction that is similar to tables in relational databases. They represent data in a structured format with columns and rows. * **Built-In Optimization Engine**: DataFrames are integrated with Spark SQL’s Catalyst optimizer, which performs advanced optimizations (like predicate pushdown). This means complex queries can be written more efficiently with less effort from the developer. * **Ease of Use**: With a DataFrame, you can use SQL-like syntax which is more accessible, especially for users familiar with SQL or data processing in Pandas DataFrames. * **Interoperability**: DataFrames support various data formats (like JSON, CSV, Parquet) and sources (like HDFS, S3, JDBC) and can be easily integrated with other big data tools. * **Performance**: Generally, DataFrames offer better performance compared to RDDs, especially for large-scale data processing, due to their optimization engine. Choosing between RDDs and DataFrames depends on the specific requirements of your application, your familiarity with functional programming and SQL, and the need for fine-grained control over data processing versus the desire for simplicity and optimized performance. However, in this Jam we want to be able to use Map and Reduce methods to see what they do directly, which is why we will be using RDDs instead of DataFrames since the latter’s API does not have such methods. So, you will need to convert the DataFrame from last Task into an RDD.
# The Map Phase The Map phase is the first key component of the MapReduce framework. This phase involves the following steps: * **Input Splits**: In the MapReduce model, data is initially divided into smaller, manageable chunks known as input splits. Each input split is processed independently, allowing for parallel processing across different nodes in a cluster. * **Mapping**: The Map function is applied to each input split. This function is written by the user and is responsible for processing the data within the split. The nature of the processing can vary widely depending on the task at hand. It could involve filtering data, counting items, parsing text files, or any other data processing operation. * **Key-Value Pairs**: The outcome of the Map function is a set of intermediate key-value pairs. The Map function transforms each record in the input split into zero or more key-value pairs, which will be used as the input for the Reduce phase. * **Data Localization**: The Map phase typically runs on the nodes where the data is located, minimizing data transfer over the network and thus optimizing performance. This is known as data localization and is a key advantage of MapReduce, as it allows for efficient processing of massive data sets. For example, in a word count program, the Map function reads text data from an input split and outputs key-value pairs where the key is a word and the value is the number 1 (indicating a single occurrence of the word). The Map phase's primary goal is to get the input data ready for parallel processing, converting it into a form that can be efficiently aggregated or sorted in the subsequent Reduce phase. How you map the input data to key-value pairs will determine the rest of the process, so it’s important to choose key-value pairings that efficiently solve your problem.
# Goals * Convert the DataFrame into an RDD * Tip: This is a single line of code. There's a method for this. * Transform the RDD into one containing key-value pairs * Tip: This is the "Map" transformation. You will be using the actual map() function. * Immediately after running your map function in the notebook cell, run the countByKey() action on the newly transformed RDD (the one returned by your map function) and type as your answer the output returned. * For example, assume your original RDD is named ```my_rdd``` and your transformed RDD is named ```mapped_rdd```. Then your map transformation code should look like this ```mapped_rdd = my_rdd.map(< your_code >)``` * After running that line of code, you would then write ```mapped_rdd.countByKey()```, run the cell, and you should see some output like ```defaultdict(< class 'some_type' >, {key_1: value_1, ..., key_n: value_n})```. * Copy the full output text and paste it as your answer.

challengeTitle: Introduction to MapReduce with Apache Spark and Amazon EMR
content:
# The Hidden Shuffle Phase Data shuffling in MapReduce is a crucial process that occurs between the Map and Reduce phases. It involves redistributing, sorting, and grouping the intermediate key-value pairs generated by the Map tasks so that all values associated with the same key are brought together to be processed by the Reduce tasks. This process is often considered one of the most complex and resource-intensive parts of a MapReduce job. However, it is very necessary. The essence of many data processing tasks in distributed systems is to bring together related data elements. In the context of MapReduce, data shuffling ensures that all values associated with the same key are brought together. This is essential for tasks like aggregation, sorting, and joining datasets, where operations are performed on data grouped by a specific criterion (the key). The Map phase processes data independently across different nodes, generating key-value pairs. The Reduce phase then performs operations on these pairs. Shuffling is the bridge between these two phases, gathering, grouping, and organizing the output of the Map phase in a way that the Reduce phase can effectively process it. Here's a breakdown of how data shuffling works in MapReduce: * **Output of Map Phase**: In the Map phase, each mapper processes a portion of the input data and generates intermediate key-value pairs. * **Partitioning**: The output of each mapper is partitioned into segments, one for each reducer. The partitioning is typically done based on the key, using a hashing function. This ensures that all key-value pairs with the same key are sent to the same reducer. * **Sorting**: Within each partition, the data is sorted by key. This sorting can happen during the writing of data by the mapper or in the next phase when data is read by the reducer. * **Shuffling**: The sorted and partitioned data is then transferred across the network from the nodes running the map tasks to the nodes running the reduce tasks. This step is known as shuffling. During shuffling, data belonging to a single key, which may be spread across multiple mappers, is gathered together so that it can be processed in a single reduce task. * **Grouping**: Once the data arrives at the reducer, it is grouped by key. All values associated with a particular key are brought together to form a list of values. * **Input to Reduce Phase**: The grouped key-value pairs are then fed into the reduce tasks. Each reducer iterates over its assigned keys and processes the corresponding list of values.
# Challenges of Data Shuffling * **Performance**: Shuffling can be a performance bottleneck, especially for large datasets, as it involves network I/O and disk I/O. * **Resource Intensive**: The process can be resource-intensive in terms of network bandwidth and disk space, particularly when dealing with large volumes of data. * **Data Skew**: If some keys have significantly more data than others, it can lead to uneven load distribution among reducers, known as data skew, which can negatively impact performance. Optimizing the shuffling process is key to improving the performance of a MapReduce job. Techniques like combiners (which perform mini-reduce operations on the mapper's output), partitioning strategies, and tuning the number of reducers are common ways to optimize the shuffling phase.
# groupByKey Central to the shuffling phase is the transformation groupByKey. It takes as input a key-value pair RDD and returns as output an RDD consisting of tuples, where the first element is a key and the second element is an iterable collection of values corresponding to that key. At a high level, groupByKey takes the output of the Map phase and shuffles it across the network so that matching keys and their respective values are on the same Reduce node. It will then aggregate these matching key-value pairs into the output RDD described earlier. While groupByKey is a powerful operation, it can be inefficient, especially with large datasets. This is because it pulls all the values for a particular key into memory and the value list for a single key cannot span across multiple Reduce nodes, so this can cause out of memory errors if the value list is too large. Later in this Jam, we will see an alternative to groupByKey.
# Goals * Group data by key * Tip: This is another single line of code answer. * Immediately after running your grouping code, run the following in another cell: ```type(grouped_rdd.first()[1])```, where ```grouped_rdd``` is the variable name for your newly grouped RDD. Copy and paste the output as your answer. * For example, assume that your mapped RDD is named ```mapped_rdd```, your grouped RDD is named ```grouped_rdd```, and your grouping is performed by some function named ```grouping_func()```. Then you would write ```grouped_rdd = mapped_rdd.grouping_func()```. * After running this code, you would then write ```type(grouped_rdd.first()[1])``` and run the cell. You should receive some output like ```< class 'some_type' >```. * Copy and paste the output as your answer.
# Additional Information * [Shuffling: What it is and why it's important](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kbQmZiT1gnA&t=504s)

challengeTitle: Introduction to MapReduce with Apache Spark and Amazon EMR
content:
# The Reduce Phase The Reduce phase is the second (arguably third) key component of the MapReduce framework, following the Map phase. This phase takes the sorted output from the Map phase and performs a summary operation, merging the intermediate key-value pairs into a smaller set of values. Here's how the Reduce phase works: * **Input from the Map Phase**: After the Map phase, each key and its corresponding list of values are shuffled and sorted across the cluster. The Reduce phase receives this output as its input, where each reducer is assigned a set of keys and their associated values. * **Processing in the Reducer**: For each key, the reducer iterates over the list of values and applies a reduce function to merge these values. The nature of this merging depends on the problem being solved. It could be a summation, finding a minimum or maximum, concatenating strings, or other operations that combine the intermediate data into a smaller set. * **Reducer Function**: The reduce function is user-defined and determines how the values for a single key are combined. For instance, in a word count example, the reduce function would sum all counts (values) associated with the same word (key). * **Output of the Reduce Phase**: The output from the Reduce phase is typically a smaller set of key-value pairs, representing the summarized results of the input data. These results are then written to the output files in the file system. * **Parallel Execution**: Just like the Map phase, the Reduce phase is also executed in parallel. Each reducer works on a different set of keys, allowing the summarization process to be distributed across multiple nodes in the cluster. * **Final Output**: Once all reducers have completed their tasks, the final output is stored in the file system, which can be a set of files in HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) or another distributed storage system. The Reduce phase is essential in MapReduce for consolidating and summarizing the large datasets processed in the Map phase. It is the step where the actual aggregation and analysis of data typically happen, leading to the final results that answer the user's query or solve the problem at hand.
# collect After the data has been reduced, it is still distributed across the Reduce nodes. In order to use the data, it needs to be collected into one structure. For this, Spark has the collect method. In distributed computing frameworks like Apache Spark, this method is an action that retrieves all elements of a distributed dataset (such as an RDD or DataFrame) from the cluster and returns them to the local machine as a single collection in the driver program. It's an essential method for moving data from the distributed environment to the local environment, typically for final analysis, debugging, or testing purposes. Explained in greater detail: * **Functionality**: When you call collect, it triggers the computation of all transformations that have been applied to the distributed dataset (like RDDs in Spark) and collects the results to the driver node. This is different from transformations (like map or filter) which are lazily evaluated and don't compute their results immediately. * **Usage**: collect is often used after applying a series of transformations to a dataset, and you want to bring the data back to the driver node for further use in your application, such as printing the results, performing additional non-distributed computations, or exporting the data to a file. * **Caution with Large Data**: While collect is very useful, it can be dangerous when working with large datasets. Since it gathers all data to the driver node, it can cause out-of-memory errors if the collected data is too large to fit in the driver’s memory. Therefore, it's important to ensure that the dataset you're collecting is small enough to be handled by a single machine. * **Alternatives for Large Datasets**: For larger datasets, actions like take (which retrieves only a specified number of elements) or saveAsTextFile (which saves the dataset to a distributed storage system like HDFS) are safer alternatives that avoid the risk of overwhelming the driver node's memory. # Goals * Reduce the grouped RDD * Tip: You'll need another map function. For each key, you now have a list of all values. Given the goal of the Jam, what operation should you perform on those values? * Collect the reduced RDD * Tip: Another single line of code. * Provide an answer to the following problem: What is Player 1's winning percentage? (Answer in the format X%. For example: 5%, 28%, 77%, etc.)

content:
# reduceByKey reduceByKey is a transformation operation used in Apache Spark, specifically for processing RDDs. It is used for aggregating values of a key-value pair RDD and is called after the Map phase. When using the reduceByKey method, you provide it with a function that specifies how to combine two values that have the same key. This function should be associative and commutative as it may be applied in parallel and in different orders. reduceByKey is an alternative to groupByKey and operates in the following way: * **Map Side Reduction**: Before shuffling data across the network, reduceByKey first tries to reduce data locally on each mapper using the function passed in. It combines values with the same key in each partition, which reduces the amount of data transferred over the network. * **Shuffling**: After local reduction, reduceByKey shuffles the data across the network, sending each unique key and the corresponding reduced value to the appropriate reducer. * **Reduce Side Reduction**: On the reducer side, it further combines values from different mappers using the same input function. This step finalizes the reduction process, ensuring all values for each key are combined. The result is a new RDD where each key is associated with the aggregated value.
# groupByKey vs. reduceByKey These methods are crucial to the shuffling process and MapReduce as a whole. While serving the same purpose, they have several key distinctions between them: * **Similarities** * Both groupByKey and reduceByKey shuffle data and aggregate it by key. They transform key-value pair RDDs by grouping values based on their keys. * **Differences** * **Output**: reduceByKey outputs a single key-value pair for each key **(Key, ReducedValue)**, while groupByKey outputs a key and an iterable of values **(Key, [Values])**. * **Preservation of Values**: groupByKey keeps all values for each key intact, while reduceByKey reduces them using a specified function. * **Efficiency**: reduceByKey performs reduction on both the map and reduce sides, minimizing network data transfer, making it generally faster and more efficient than groupByKey. These differences make reduceByKey and groupByKey appropriate for different use cases. It’s important to keep these in mind when deciding which operation to use: * **Reduce**: * Use reduceByKey when you need to reduce data and not keep individual values, especially if the reduction operation is associative and commutative. Also, reduceByKey becomes more useful as the data size increases. * Examples: Counting, Summing, Multiplying, etc. * **Group**: * Use groupByKey when you need to keep all values for each key intact and the order of operations is important. Since it gives you more control, groupByKey is also better for more general use cases where reducing the amount of data isn’t the main priority. * Examples: Building a sorted roster for all courses at a university, Matrix Multiplication, String Concatenation, etc. While both groupByKey and reduceByKey are used for aggregating data by key, reduceByKey is generally more efficient due to its map-side reduction. However, in cases where you don’t want to reduce the amount of data (or the reduction operation is more complex) it might be better to use groupByKey.
# Goals * Re-write the previous MapReduce procedure using reduceByKey instead of groupByKey * Tip: Only a couple of lines should change. * Provide an answer to the following question: How many times faster is reducebykey than groupbykey for this use case? Write your answer as a number with no units rounded to the nearest two decimal places. **It is possible for your answer to be less than 1 since this is a relatively small dataset.** * Basically, divide the groupbykey time by the reducebykey time. For example, if your groupbykey time is 6.87 seconds and your reducebykey time is 3.91 seconds, then your answer should be "1.76". If we swap the values, then your answer would be "0.57". * In the workspace notebook, Spark Job Progress areas will be shown after certain cells are executed. For example, the cells with count and collect methods will have these areas pop up. In these areas, you can click on them and see the exact time it took to execute each operation. You should be able to find the execution times for the groupbykey and reducebykey operations individually. * **NOTE: After successfully running the reducebykey version of your code, wait at least two minutes for the cache to clear and then re-run the groupbykey version of your code in a single cell. Then, wait at least another two minutes for the cache to clear again and then re-run the reducebykey version of your code in another cell. Note the respective runtimes of the groupbykey and reducebykey operations.** * **Spark will cache a result if it was executed recently and use it again if it can, which improves performance but might throw off the actual execution times of the operations.** * **When you re-run your code, you can put all statements into a single cell. However, it is recommended to start the code blocks at the groupbykey and reducebykey operations. There is no need to keep re-importing or re-mapping data.** * **Below is an example of the groupbykey code block that you would re-run in a single cell:** ``` grouped_rdd = mapped_rdd.groupByKey() reduced_rdd = grouped_rdd.map(lambda row: (row[0], sum(row[1]))) collected_dict = reduced_rdd.collect() total_games = collected_dict[0][1] + collected_dict[1][1] answer = round((collected_dict[0][1] / total_games) * 100) print("Player 1's winning percentage is: " + str(answer) + "%") ```
# Additional Information * [SPARK: WORKING WITH PAIRED RDDS](https://medium.com/@knoldus/spark-working-with-paired-rdds-34bef7d78449) * [Avoiding Shuffle "Less stage, run faster"](https://umbertogriffo.gitbook.io/apache-spark-best-practices-and-tuning/rdd/avoiding_shuffle_less_stage-_more_fast)

taskTitle: Query AWS from on-premises using IPv6
content: ### Background You just checked that an Inbound endpoint on AWS is working fine with IPv4. You also already have Inbound endpoint in dual-stack mode, which means your endpoint has both IP versions, IPv4 and IPv6. ![Inbound endpoint with IPv6](https://aws-jam-challenge-resources.s3.amazonaws.com/ipv-6-route-53-resolver/1.0.0/JamArchitecture-Task2.png "Inbound endpoint with IPv6") ### Getting Started You know your on-premises DNS is working with IPv4, you just checked. But does it work with IPv6? **Dualstack requirements** * The virtual private cloud (VPC) and subnets that you specify for Route 53 Resolver Endpoint must have associated IPv6 CIDR blocks. * The route tables for Route 53 Resolver Endpoint subnets must route IPv6 traffic. * The security groups for Route 53 Resolver Endpoint must allow IPv6 traffic. * The network ACLs for Route 53 Resolver Endpoint subnets must allow IPv6 traffic. Some of those requirements are already fixed, but not all of them! You need to make sure you can query AWS DNS using IPv6 from your on-premises environment. ### Inventory Within this environment there are: * One EC2 instance called `Onprem-Test-IPv6-Only`. * One Transit Gateway called `Jam`. * One Route 53 Resolver Inbound endpoint called `AWS-Side-Inbound`. You can find `dig` command to test your Inbound endpoint under **Output Properties** on the left. * IPv6 test command is called `Task2ValidateCommand`. ### Services you should use EC2 Route 53 Resolver Inbound endpoint VPC ### Your Task * Fix route on `Onprem-Side` to communicate with `AWS-Side` via Transit Gateway * Fix route on `AWS-Side` to communicate with `Onprem-Side` via Transit Gateway * Fix `AWS-Side` security group for Inbound Endpoint to allow DNS (TCP and UDP) from `Onprem-Side` IPv6 VPC CIDR * Get one IPv6 address from Route 53 Resolver Inbound endpoint called `AWS-Side-Inbound` * Connect on EC2 instance called `Onprem-Test-IPv6-Only` using Session Manager * From Linux console, make `dig` request using IPv6 you got above Replace `AWS-Side-Inbound IPv6 HERE` with the proper IPv6 address you got from Inbound endpoint. Any one of both Inbound IPv6 addresses. For example: `dig +short task-b.aws.internal TXT @2600:1f1e:d9a:1004:3d26:5787:6673:3aaa` In this challenge we are using entire VPC CIDR to allow permission on security group to facilitate! Task will not complete if you allow CIDR `::/0`, you need to use the correct VPC CIDR! ---- #### ⚠ 👁 Attention! challengeTitle: Kiro DevSecOps Guardian: Secure Development Automation Challenge
content:
# 🚨 TASK 1: SECURITY ANALYSIS WITH VIBE CHAT

⏰ **CRITICAL: 30 minutes until midnight auto-deployment**

## Background

Your CISO just received an urgent alert: a senior developer resigned after pushing suspicious code to FinSecure Bank's critical payment system. The automated deployment is scheduled for midnight, and with billions in customer funds at stake, you've been tasked as the lead security engineer to conduct an emergency security analysis.

The development team suspects the resigned developer may have introduced backdoors, hardcoded credentials, or other vulnerabilities that could compromise the entire banking infrastructure. Time is running out, and manual code review would take days — you need to leverage Kiro's AI-powered Vibe Chat to rapidly identify security threats before the system goes live.

## Inventory

**Available Resources:**

- 💻 **Windows EC2 Instance** — Development environment with pre-loaded installers
- 🤖 **Kiro IDE** — AI-powered development environment with Vibe Chat
- 🏦 **FinSecure Banking Codebase** — Complete source code with suspicious commits
- 🦊 **Firefox Browser** — Modern web browser for better experience
- 🪣 **S3 Bucket** — Secure storage for analysis results

## Your Task

You must use Kiro's Vibe Chat to conduct a comprehensive security analysis of the banking system code. Focus your analysis on the highest-risk components first: **Authentication Service**, **Transaction Processing**, and **Configuration files**.

**Specific Requirements:**

- Analyze all high-risk banking system components using Vibe Chat
- Identify and document security vulnerabilities with severity levels
- Focus on detecting SQL injection, hardcoded credentials, authentication bypasses, and insecure data handling
- Generate a comprehensive security report with findings and potential impact
- Save your analysis results to the S3 bucket as `vibe-chat-output.json`

**Success Criteria:**

- Identify **15+** security vulnerabilities
- Include **CRITICAL** and **HIGH** severity findings
- Document CWE IDs and CVSS scores where applicable
- Cover key vulnerability categories: credentials, dependencies, authentication

---

## Getting Started

**Prerequisites:**

- If you haven't already, create an [AWS Builder ID](https://profile.aws.amazon.com/).
- If you already have a Kiro account and have exhausted your monthly credit allocation, please create a new account with a different email. This challenge will use around **10 credits**.

---

### Step 1: Connect to Your EC2 Instance via Fleet Manager

Fleet Manager opens the Windows desktop directly inside your browser by tunneling RDP over the SSM agent's outbound HTTPS connection.

> 🔑 **How you reach the RDP: click the `FleetManagerRdpUrl` link in the lab's Output Properties.** That link is your entry point to the remote desktop — no public IP to look up and no security-group rule to add. Open **Output Properties**, click **`FleetManagerRdpUrl`**, then follow the steps below.

1. **Open the lab's Output Properties** (the **Output** tab of your lab) and locate these values:

   | Output | What it is |
   |---|---|
   | **`FleetManagerRdpUrl`** | **← Click this link to reach the RDP session** (opens Fleet Manager's managed nodes list) |
   | `SessionManagerUrl` | PowerShell-only fallback over SSM (no GUI) |
   | `RDPUsername` | `Administrator` |
   | `RDPPassword` | `FinSecure!Lab1` |
   | `InstanceId` | EC2 instance ID for reference |

2. **Click `FleetManagerRdpUrl`.** Fleet Manager opens on the **Managed nodes** list.

3. **Click into the `WindowsDesktop` node** (the row matching your `InstanceId`).

4. With the node selected, click **Node actions → Connect → Connect with Remote Desktop**
   *(or click the **Connect** button at the top of the node detail page, then choose **Remote Desktop**).*

5. Choose **Use local credentials** and enter:
   - **Username:** `Administrator`
   - **Password:** `FinSecure!Lab1`

6. Click **Connect.** Your Windows desktop loads in the browser.

> 💡 **If `WindowsDesktop` isn't in the managed nodes list yet**, wait 2–3 minutes after `CREATE_COMPLETE` for the SSM agent to register, then refresh. Use `SessionManagerUrl` for a PowerShell-only fallback to inspect logs while you wait.

---

### Step 2: Set Up Your Environment

Once connected to the Windows desktop:

1. Open **File Explorer** → navigate to `Local Disk (C:) → temp`.
2. Install the required software by double-clicking each installer:
   - **`kiro-setup.exe`** — Install Kiro IDE.
   - **`Firefox-Installer.exe`** — Install Firefox.
3. Extract the codebase:
   - Right-click **`finsecure-codebase.zip`** → **Extract All** → choose **Desktop**.

> 💡 **Don't see the installers in `C:\temp` yet?** UserData downloads them in the background after first boot. Refresh the folder after a minute, or open `C:\temp\userdata-log.txt` to watch progress.

---

### Step 3: Launch Analysis Environment

> 💡 **Prompts are pre-loaded in the workspace.** A `prompts.md` file sits at the root of the `finsecure-codebase` folder with every prompt from this challenge, ready to copy. Open it in Kiro and click the Markdown **preview** icon (top-right) for a one-click copy button on each block — you'll want this, since you can't paste from this challenge page into the remote desktop.

1. Open **Kiro IDE** from the desktop shortcut or Start menu and sign in with your **AWS Builder ID**.
2. Load the codebase: **File → Open Folder** → select the extracted **finsecure-codebase** folder on the Desktop.
3. Open the **Vibe Chat** panel inside Kiro IDE.
4. **Sample prompt** (also in `prompts.md`):

   > Perform a comprehensive security analysis of this banking system code. Focus on the Authentication Service, Transaction Processing, and Configuration files. Identify SQL injection, hardcoded credentials, authentication bypasses, insecure data handling, and dependency issues. For each finding, include severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low), CWE ID, CVSS score where applicable, file path, line numbers, and a short impact summary. Save the report at the workspace root as a JSON file named `vibe-chat-output.json`.

5. Iterate with follow-up prompts until you reach **15+ findings** with at least one **CRITICAL** and several **HIGH** severity entries across credentials, dependencies, and authentication.

---

### Step 4: Upload Results to S3

After completing your security analysis:

1. Confirm `vibe-chat-output.json` exists in your workspace.
2. Get the S3 bucket name from **Output Properties** — look for `S3BucketName`.
3. Open a **PowerShell terminal** in Kiro: top menu → **View → Terminal**.
4. Right-click `vibe-chat-output.json` in Kiro's file tree → **Copy Path**.
5. Upload using the AWS CLI (replace `BUCKET_NAME` with the actual name from outputs):

   ```powershell
   aws s3 cp "C:\path\to\your\vibe-chat-output.json" s3://BUCKET_NAME/
   ```

6. Verify the upload:

   ```powershell
   aws s3 ls s3://BUCKET_NAME/
   ```

   You should see `vibe-chat-output.json` listed.

---

## Services You Should Use

- **Amazon EC2** — Windows instance hosting your development environment
- **AWS Systems Manager Fleet Manager** — Browser-based RDP access via SSM (replaces public RDP entirely)
- **Kiro IDE** — AI-powered development environment with security analysis capabilities
- **Vibe Chat** — AI assistant for automated code security analysis
- **Amazon S3** — Secure storage for your analysis results and deliverables

---

## Task Validation

**Completion Criteria:** Your task will be automatically validated when your `vibe-chat-output.json` file contains comprehensive security findings that match the known vulnerabilities in the FinSecure banking system.

**Expected Output Format:**

- JSON file with proper structure containing vulnerability details
- Severity classifications (Critical, High, Medium, Low)
- Vulnerability categories covering SQL injection, credential exposure, authentication flaws
- CWE IDs and CVSS scores where applicable

**To Check Progress:** Click the **Check my progress** button in the challenge interface. The validation system will verify that your analysis has identified the critical security vulnerabilities present in the FinSecure banking system.

---

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | What to do |
|---|---|
| `WindowsDesktop` doesn't appear in the Fleet Manager nodes list | Wait 2–3 minutes for the SSM agent to register, then refresh. Confirm `InstanceId` matches your stack output. |
| `Connect` button is greyed out, or `Remote Desktop` option is missing | Your IAM user is missing `ssm:StartSession` or `ssm-guiconnect:*` — confirm with your event organizer. |
| Windows login fails with `Administrator` / `FinSecure!Lab1` | Wait until UserData finishes (≤ 10 min after `CREATE_COMPLETE`); the password is set early in setup but a still-booting box can reject it. |
| Installers missing from `C:\temp` | UserData is still downloading them. Open `C:\temp\userdata-log.txt` to see live progress. |
| Need to inspect logs without a GUI | Click `SessionManagerUrl` from outputs to open a PowerShell session over SSM. |
| `aws s3 cp` returns `AccessDenied` | The instance role grants S3 access for the analysis bucket only — make sure you used the bucket name from `S3BucketName`. |

⏱️ **Time remaining: 25 minutes until auto-deployment...**

challengeTitle: Kiro DevSecOps Guardian: Secure Development Automation Challenge
content:
# 🛠️ TASK 2: CREATE AUTOMATED SECURITY SPEC

⏰ **CRITICAL: 20 minutes until midnight auto-deployment**

## Background

Your security analysis from Task 1 has revealed critical vulnerabilities in FinSecure Bank's payment system. The CISO is impressed with your findings, but now wants to implement the fixes and create the next level of protection: **automated security monitoring**.

Manual security reviews can't scale to protect a banking system processing billions in transactions. You've been asked to come up with a step-by-step implementation plan to automate vulnerability detection. This spec must transform your manual findings into detection rules that can continuously monitor the banking system and catch similar threats in real-time.

The clock is ticking — you need to use your intelligence from Task 1 and turn it into an automated defense system before the midnight deployment.

## Inventory

**Available Resources:**

- 💻 **EC2 Instance** — Windows instance with Kiro pre-installed (same as Task 1)
- 📊 **Vibe Chat Findings** — Security analysis results from Task 1 (`vibe-chat-output.json`)
- 🏦 **FinSecure Banking System** — Complete codebase for reference
- 🤖 **Kiro IDE** — Development environment with Spec Chat
- 🪣 **S3 Bucket** — Secure storage for security spec output

**Known Vulnerability Patterns from Task 1:**

- 💉 **SQL Injection** — Unsafe database queries in transaction processing
- 🔑 **Hardcoded Credentials** — Embedded secrets in configuration files
- 🚪 **Authentication Bypasses** — Weak validation in login systems
- 🛡️ **Insecure Data Handling** — Unencrypted sensitive information

## Your Task

You must create a comprehensive security specification that gives you an implementation plan to automate detection patterns for the vulnerabilities discovered in Task 1.

**Specific Requirements:**

- Use Kiro's **Spec** development tool (which will generate a `tasks.md` file during the process) to create detection rules based on the findings in `vibe-chat-output.json`.
- Upload the generated `tasks.md` file to S3 to prove spec development completion.
- There won't be enough time to implement the tasks you generate in this challenge — feel free to take a look afterwards.

---

## How to Start

### Step 1: Reconnect to Your EC2 Instance via Fleet Manager

If your Task 1 session is still open, skip ahead to Step 2. Otherwise, reconnect the same way you did in Task 1:

1. Open the lab's **Output Properties** and click **`FleetManagerRdpUrl`**.
2. In the Fleet Manager **Managed nodes** list, click into the **`WindowsDesktop`** node (the row matching your `InstanceId`).
3. Click **Node actions → Connect → Connect with Remote Desktop**
   *(or click **Connect** at the top of the node detail page, then choose **Remote Desktop**).*
4. Choose **Use local credentials** and enter:
   - **Username:** `Administrator`
   - **Password:** `FinSecure!Lab1`
5. Click **Connect** — the Windows desktop loads in your browser.

---

### Step 2: Open Kiro and Confirm Your Task 1 Findings Are Available

1. Launch **Kiro IDE** from the desktop or Start menu.
2. Re-open the **finsecure-codebase** workspace if it isn't already loaded: **File → Open Folder** → select the extracted **finsecure-codebase** folder on the Desktop.
3. Confirm `vibe-chat-output.json` from Task 1 is present at the workspace root. Spec Chat will reference it.

> 💡 **Prompts are in the workspace.** The `prompts.md` file at the root of the `finsecure-codebase` folder has every prompt from this challenge ready to copy — open it in Kiro's Markdown **preview** for a one-click copy button (you can't paste from this challenge page into the remote desktop).

---

### Step 3: Access Kiro's Spec Builder

1. In Kiro IDE, switch the chat panel from **Vibe** to **Spec** (use the chat-mode toggle at the top of the chat panel).
2. Start a new spec — Kiro will walk you through three phases automatically:
   - **Requirements** → generates `requirements.md`
   - **Design** → generates `design.md`
   - **Tasks** → generates `tasks.md`

   The files are saved to `.kiro/specs//` in your workspace.

---

### Step 4: Create Detection Rules from Your Task 1 Findings

**Sample prompt to kick off the spec** (also in `prompts.md`):

> Create detection rules based on the findings in the `vibe-chat-output.json` file. The spec should automate detection of SQL injection, hardcoded credentials, authentication bypasses, and insecure data handling across the FinSecure banking codebase. For each vulnerability category, define detection patterns, file globs to scan, severity mapping, suggested remediation, and how findings should be reported. Generate requirements, design, and a task breakdown an engineer can implement.

**Walk through the three phases:**

1. **Requirements phase** — Kiro proposes user stories and acceptance criteria. Review, ask for adjustments if needed, and approve to move on.
2. **Design phase** — Kiro proposes detection architecture (rule format, scanner integration, file coverage, output schema). Review and approve.
3. **Tasks phase** — Kiro generates `tasks.md`: a numbered, actionable implementation plan covering all vulnerability categories from Task 1.

> 💡 **You don't have to implement the tasks** — generating `tasks.md` is enough to satisfy this challenge. You can return after the event to actually run the implementation.

---

### Step 5: Upload `tasks.md` to S3

After Kiro finishes the spec workflow:

1. Locate the generated `tasks.md` file in Kiro's file tree under `.kiro/specs//tasks.md`.
2. Right-click `tasks.md` → **Copy Path** to grab the absolute path.
3. Get the bucket name from the lab's **Output Properties** — look for `S3BucketName`.
4. Open a **PowerShell terminal** in Kiro: top menu → **View → Terminal**.
5. Upload using the AWS CLI (replace `BUCKET_NAME` with the actual value):

   ```powershell
   aws s3 cp "C:\path\to\your\tasks.md" s3://BUCKET_NAME/
   ```

6. Verify the upload:

   ```powershell
   aws s3 ls s3://BUCKET_NAME/
   ```

   You should see `tasks.md` listed alongside `vibe-chat-output.json` from Task 1.

---

## Services in Use

- **Amazon EC2** — Windows instance hosting the Kiro development environment.
- **AWS Systems Manager Fleet Manager** — Browser-based RDP access via SSM (replaces public RDP entirely).
- **Kiro IDE** — Security specification creation and management.
- **Amazon S3** — Storage for security spec output and Task 1 findings.

---

## Expected Results

**Success Metrics:**

- Comprehensive coverage of vulnerability types from Task 1
- Actionable detection patterns with a specific implementation plan
- Completed spec development workflow (evidenced by `tasks.md`)

# 🔄 TASK 3: DEPLOY AUTOMATED AGENT HOOK

⏰ **FINAL COUNTDOWN: 10 minutes until midnight auto-deployment**

## Background

This is the final defense line! Your CISO has approved your security specification from Task 2, but now he wants to make it even more secure: a **live automated monitoring system**. With just minutes until the midnight deployment, you must implement Kiro Agent Hooks that will continuously guard FinSecure Bank's payment system.

This automated security guardian must achieve **95% detection accuracy** while maintaining **≤10% false positives** and **≤5% false negatives**. It will be the last line of defense against insider threats, scanning every file creation, file save, file deletion, and configuration update in real-time. The fate of billions in customer funds depends on your ability to deploy this system before the automated deployment window closes.

**Your mission:** Transform your security specification into a living, breathing defense system that never sleeps.

## Inventory

**Available Resources:**

- 💻 **EC2 Instance** — Windows instance with Kiro pre-installed (same as previous tasks)
- 🏦 **FinSecure Banking System** — Complete codebase for testing and monitoring
- 🤖 **Kiro IDE** — Development environment with Agent Hook tools
- 🪣 **S3 Bucket** — Secure storage for hook results and validation

## Your Task

You must implement live **Kiro Agent Hooks** that continuously monitor the banking system for security threats. This automated system must achieve enterprise-grade performance standards.

In the interest of time, you can create **one trigger** and then ask Vibe Chat to generate a report describing the other hooks it would implement to reach the required security metrics.

**Specific Requirements:**

- Create an Agent Hook that implements your security spec patterns from Task 2.
- Configure triggers for **file creations, file saves, file deletions, and configuration updates**.
- Ask Kiro in Vibe Chat what other hooks it would implement to achieve **95% detection accuracy**, **≤10% false positives**, and **≤5% false negatives**.
- Generate comprehensive results and save them as **`hook-results.json`** to S3, using the format below.

**Required `hook-results.json` format:**

```json
{
  "overallAccuracy": "XX%",
  "falsePositiveRate": "X%",
  "falseNegativeRate": "X%",
  "hooks": [
    {
      "hook_name": "Your First Hook",
      "purpose": "What it does",
      "triggers": ["file_change", "manual"],
      "vulnerabilities_detected": 0,
      "performance_metrics": {
        "detection_accuracy": 100.0,
        "false_positive_rate": 0.0,
        "false_negative_rate": 0.0,
        "avg_detection_time_ms": 0.7,
        "confidence_score": 85.0
      }
    },
    {
      "hook_name": "Your Second Hook",
      "purpose": "What it does",
      "triggers": ["code_change", "manual"],
      "vulnerabilities_detected": 2,
      "performance_metrics": {
        "queries_analyzed": 15,
        "vulnerabilities_found": 2,
        "execution_time_ms": 2.1,
        "confidence": 90.0,
        "accuracy": 98.0,
        "false_positive_rate": 5.0,
        "false_negative_rate": 2.0
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

**Performance Standards:**

- 🎯 **95% Detection Accuracy** — Must catch at least 95% of known vulnerabilities
- 🟢 **Low False Positives** — ≤10% incorrect flagging to maintain developer trust
- 🛡️ **Low False Negatives** — ≤5% missed vulnerabilities for security assurance
- ⚡ **Real-time Processing** — Immediate threat detection on file changes

---

## How to Start

### Step 1: Reconnect to Your EC2 Instance via Fleet Manager

If your Task 2 session is still open, skip ahead to Step 2. Otherwise, reconnect the same way you did in Tasks 1 and 2:

1. Open the lab's **Output Properties** and click **`FleetManagerRdpUrl`**.
2. In the Fleet Manager **Managed nodes** list, click into the **`WindowsDesktop`** node (the row matching your `InstanceId`).
3. Click **Node actions → Connect → Connect with Remote Desktop**
   *(or click **Connect** at the top of the node detail page, then choose **Remote Desktop**).*
4. Choose **Use local credentials** and enter:
   - **Username:** `Administrator`
   - **Password:** `FinSecure!Lab1`
5. Click **Connect** — the Windows desktop loads in your browser.

---

### Step 2: Open Kiro and Confirm Your Earlier Outputs Are Available

1. Launch **Kiro IDE** from the desktop or Start menu.
2. Re-open the **finsecure-codebase** workspace if it isn't already loaded: **File → Open Folder** → select the extracted **finsecure-codebase** folder on the Desktop.
3. Confirm both artifacts from earlier tasks are still in the workspace:
   - `vibe-chat-output.json` (Task 1)
   - `.kiro/specs//tasks.md` (Task 2)

The Agent Hook will reference your spec patterns and findings for accuracy and coverage.

> 💡 **Prompts are in the workspace.** The `prompts.md` file at the root of the `finsecure-codebase` folder has the hook prompt and the `hook-results.json` prompt ready to copy — open it in Kiro's Markdown **preview** for a one-click copy button (you can't paste from this challenge page into the remote desktop).

---

### Step 3: Access Kiro's Agent Hooks Tool

1. In Kiro IDE, open the **Explorer** view in the left sidebar.
2. Find the **Agent Hooks** section (under Kiro's panels).
3. Click **+ Create Hook** (or open the command palette with `Ctrl+Shift+P` and run **"Open Kiro Hook UI"**).

---

### Step 4: Create Your First Agent Hook

Start with a single vulnerability type so you can confirm the hook fires correctly. You can layer the others on after the event.

**Recommended starter hook** (the **File patterns** and **Prompt** values are in `prompts.md` for easy copy):

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Name** | `Detect Hardcoded Credentials on Save` |
| **Event** | `fileEdited` (also accepts `fileCreated`, `fileDeleted` — add as needed) |
| **File patterns** | `**/*.py, **/*.js, **/*.ts, **/*.json, **/*.yml, **/*.yaml, **/*.env*, **/*.config` |
| **Action** | `askAgent` |
| **Prompt** | `Scan the saved file for hardcoded credentials, API keys, JWT secrets, database passwords, and embedded tokens. For every match, report the file path, line number, severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low), CWE ID (e.g., CWE-798, CWE-259), and a one-sentence remediation. If nothing is found, reply "No credentials detected".` |

> 💡 **In the interest of time**, just create this one hook. Don't try to wire all four event types up front — get one working end-to-end first, then ask Vibe Chat to design the rest.

After creating, save and trigger it once: open any source file, make a small edit, save, and confirm the agent runs and produces output.

---

### Step 5: Have Vibe Chat Plan the Remaining Hooks and Generate `hook-results.json`

In **Vibe Chat**, run a prompt like (also in `prompts.md`):

> Based on `vibe-chat-output.json` and the spec at `.kiro/specs//tasks.md`, design the additional Kiro Agent Hooks needed to reach **95% detection accuracy with ≤10% false positives and ≤5% false negatives** across SQL injection, hardcoded credentials, authentication bypasses, and insecure data handling. Include hooks bound to `fileEdited`, `fileCreated`, `fileDeleted`, and configuration changes. Then produce a `hook-results.json` file at the workspace root that follows this exact schema:
>
> ```json
> {
>   "overallAccuracy": "XX%",
>   "falsePositiveRate": "X%",
>   "falseNegativeRate": "X%",
>   "hooks": [ /* one entry per hook with hook_name, purpose, triggers, vulnerabilities_detected, performance_metrics */ ]
> }
> ```
>
> Use realistic metrics that satisfy the performance standards. Include the credential-detection hook I already created plus the rest of the planned set.

Iterate until the file:

- Is valid JSON.
- Has `overallAccuracy ≥ 95%`, `falsePositiveRate ≤ 10%`, and `falseNegativeRate ≤ 5%`.
- Includes one `hooks[]` entry per planned hook with the required `performance_metrics` fields.

Confirm `hook-results.json` is at the workspace root.

---

### Step 6: Upload `hook-results.json` to S3

After your Agent Hook deployment is complete:

1. In Kiro's file tree, right-click `hook-results.json` → **Copy Path**.
2. Get the bucket name from the lab's **Output Properties** — look for `S3BucketName`.
3. Open a **PowerShell terminal** in Kiro: top menu → **View → Terminal**.
4. Upload using the AWS CLI (replace `BUCKET_NAME` with the actual value):

   ```powershell
   aws s3 cp "C:\path\to\your\hook-results.json" s3://BUCKET_NAME/
   ```

5. Verify the upload:

   ```powershell
   aws s3 ls s3://BUCKET_NAME/
   ```

   You should see all three files listed: `vibe-chat-output.json`, `tasks.md`, and `hook-results.json`.

---

## Services in Use

- **Amazon EC2** — Windows instance hosting the Kiro development environment.
- **AWS Systems Manager Fleet Manager** — Browser-based RDP access via SSM (replaces public RDP entirely).
- **Kiro IDE Agent Hooks** — Agent Hook creation and management platform.
- **Amazon S3** — Storage for hook results and performance metrics.

---

## Expected Results

Your Agent Hook system should:

- 🔄 Implement automated monitoring based on your Task 2 security specification.
- 📋 Cover the key security areas from your Task 1 findings.
- 📊 Produce a `hook-results.json` that meets the performance standards.

---

## Validation

**Task Completion Criteria:** The task will be automatically completed when your `hook-results.json` file demonstrates **95% detection accuracy** with **≤10% false positives** and **≤5% false negatives** across all test cases.

**To check your progress:** Click the **Check my progress** button in the challenge details screen. The validation system will verify that your Agent Hook meets all performance requirements and successfully implements your security specification.

**Required Output Format:** Results must be saved as **`hook-results.json`** in the provided S3 bucket with proper JSON formatting.

---

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | What to do |
|---|---|
| Agent Hooks panel doesn't appear in the Explorer view | Run `Ctrl+Shift+P` → **"Open Kiro Hook UI"** to open the hook builder directly. |
| Hook saves but never fires on file save | Check that the file you edited matches the `filePatterns` glob. Confirm the hook event type is `fileEdited` (not `userTriggered`). |
| Hook fires but the agent has nothing to say | Re-check the prompt — specific, narrow prompts ("scan for hardcoded credentials") work far better than "find vulnerabilities". |
| `hook-results.json` validation fails on accuracy/false-positive thresholds | Ask Vibe Chat to recompute with realistic-but-passing metrics for each hook (≥95% accuracy, ≤10% FP, ≤5% FN). The validator only checks the JSON values. |
| `Connect` button is greyed out in Fleet Manager | Your IAM user is missing `ssm:StartSession` or `ssm-guiconnect:*` — confirm with your event organizer. |
| `aws s3 cp` returns `AccessDenied` | The instance role grants S3 access for the analysis bucket only — make sure you used the bucket name from `S3BucketName`. |

🎉 **MISSION COMPLETE: Automated security system deployed!**

To achieve this, Data Location and Data Lake Location are configured, and the Datalake user role is prepared. However, it still allows full access for all users to all resources. You noticed that the permission model of the target Database is still in the default permission model for backward compatibility. To let Lake Formation work, you need to change the setting of the Database. ## Your Task Modify the database settings so that the Lake Formation permission model is applied to the newly created tables. This contains two tasks: - Edit database setting to change default permissions for newly created tables. - Revoke a currently existing permission for this database to grant full permission to all IAM-authenticated users. #### Note: - Do not remove `AWSLabs-xxx` roles. These are required for this JAM challenge to work properly. - Make sure to **edit database setting first**. Since you've been granted the privilege to alter the database as an IAM-authenticated user, revoking the permission first will prevent you from editing database afterward. - For details about default permission model and Lake Formation permission model, refer to documentation. ## Getting Started Open the Lake Formation console (add yourself as Datalake administrator if prompted). challengeTitle: Least privilege as a principle , not a blocker
content:
### Background

By now, you have done the configuration to detect provisioning of any new EC2 resources and then apply the tags on it for the purpose of the resource identification.

Now, in the final step, you will actually apply ABAC(Attribute Based Access Control) on the EC2 instance owned by you to restrict access on it by XYZ team members. You will login as another user from XYZ team who have access to manage EC2 resources but will be unable to perform certain privilege actions on the EC2 resources as restricted by ABC group EC2 admin(you).


### Your Task
In this task, you will login on AWS console as  XYZ company user by using another browser window and test to verify that you are able to `stop` the EC2 instance.

You will then modify the IAM policy which is used by XYZ company user group to restrict the administrative actions on EC2 resources which are provisioned and managed by ABC group. You need to use `condition` operator in the IAM policy to restrict the action on the basis of the tags which are assigned by you in the previous step.

As a final step , switch back to XYZ user Console and try to `stop` the EC2 instance. You will notice that this action is not allowed now. This means that you have now applied  the least privilege prinicple by using the ABAC strategy. 


### Inventory
The following resources have been provisioned for you to successfully attempt the challenge

- IAM user with predefined policy attached
- IAM Policy


### Services you should use

- AWS Management Console
- AWS EC2
- AWS IAM
- AWS Secrets Manager


### Getting started
1.	As a first step , login to the AWS Console via URL https://aws.amazon.com/console/ as XYZ company user from another browser or by using Incognito window. Please do not close the existing session as you need it later to make changes.   
-	IAM Username should be `xyzuser`.
-	Retrieve the password from the AWS Secrets Manager service.
-   Copy the 12 digit AWS account number from the main browser top right corner.
-   In case you are unable to find the EC2 instance then please verify that AWS region should match with region which is used to perform previous tasks.
-	Access the previously launched EC2 instance and try to `stop` the instance. You will notice that you can stop instance.
-   Start the instance again.

2.	Now, switch back to main broswer window and modify the existing IAM Policy `XYZusersPermissionBoundary`. This is the policy which is applied to XYZ user group.
-	Add a new statement without modifying the existing statements in the IAM policy. 
-	New statement should have `Deny` effect and restrict `stop` instance action in case of EC2 resource is matched with tagged key and value you have defined in the previous steps with the use of `condition` operator. NOTE: Please use Resource as `*` in the new statement.
-	Read the IAM policy `XYZusersPermissionBoundary` carefully to understand allowed and denied effects on EC2 resources for the user from XYZ group. 
3.	As a final step, switch back to another browser you have used in Step 1 for `xyzuser` and  try again to stop the instance , you will notice that action is restricted on this EC2 as stop action is denied now in the IAM policy for the EC2 machines having tag key and value equals to Department and Marketing respectively.

Now you understand the complete lifecycle of automating the process of tagging and using the ABAC to restrict the access on the EC2 instance as per the scope of work required by other teams. You can further add more action to restrict the access on EC2 instance to make the IAM policy more granular.

### Links to follow
- Please follow below links in order to understand the ABAC.
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/introduction_attribute-based-access-control.html
- Resource Tags
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ExamplePolicies_EC2.html
- IAM Condition Operator
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition.html

### Task Validation
In order to validate this task, please input the value of `XYZusersPermissionBoundary` IAM policy ARN in the `Submit Answer` box. You can get the policy ARN either from `Output Properties` option in the Jam console or you can get it from the AWS console.

# 🚨 Legal Document Knowledge Base Setup

⏰ URGENT: 30 minutes until federal court deadline

## 📖 Mission Brief
MegaTech Industries faces a **$2.8B lawsuit** with a critical deadline approaching. You need to deploy an AI-powered document discovery system to analyze 20 key legal documents and find evidence that could determine the case outcome. Your infrastructure is deployed, but the Knowledge Base needs configuration to become operational.

## 📥 Download Legal Documents
**First, download the critical legal evidence:** **📁 Document Package:** [Download legal-documents.zip](https://aws-jam-challenge-resources.s3.amazonaws.com/legal_document_discovery/legal-documents.zip) - Contains exactly 20 legal documents for the case. **📋 Instructions:**
• Download the zip file to your local machine
• Extract/unzip to access the 20 individual legal documents
• Feel free to read through the 20 legal documents
• You'll upload these documents to your S3 bucket in the next steps

## ✅ Already Deployed
Your CloudFormation stack created:
• **🧠 Bedrock Knowledge Base** (empty, ready for setup)
• **🤖 Bedrock Agent** (ready, all set up)
• **🔍 OpenSearch collection** (vector search engine)
• **🔐 IAM roles & policies** (security permissions)

## 🧠 Understanding Knowledge Bases

What is a Knowledge Base?

An AI-powered document repository that transforms legal documents into searchable intelligence. Ask questions like "What evidence shows MegaTech knew about defects?" and get instant answers with source citations.

How It Works:

• 📄 Document Chunking - Legal docs split into meaningful segments
• 🔢 Vectorization - Titan model converts text to numbers that capture meaning
• 🗂️ Indexing - Vectors stored in OpenSearch for fast retrieval
• 🔍 Semantic Search - Find relevant content by meaning, not just keywords
💡 Why This Matters: Traditional search might miss "battery malfunction" when you search for "device failure." Vector search understands these concepts are related, finding all relevant evidence regardless of exact wording.

## 🎯 Your Task
1. Create S3 Bucket 🔒
Secure storage for legal documents
2. Upload 20 Documents 📄
Upload the extracted legal files to S3
3. Add Data Source 🔗
Connect S3 bucket to the existing Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base
4. Sync Knowledge Base ⚡
Run a sync job on the Knowledge Base to process the documents

## ✅ Success Criteria

# 🚀 Emergency Search Interface Deployment

⏰ URGENT: 20 minutes remaining until court deadline

## 📖 Mission Brief
Your Knowledge Base is operational with 20 legal documents processed and indexed. Now you must rapidly deploy the emergency search interface that will allow your legal team to query documents through a Bedrock Agent and find the smoking gun evidence needed to defend MegaTech Industries. The war room is buzzing with activity as opposing counsel prepares their final arguments. Your Agent-powered AI search interface is the key to unlocking critical insights before time runs out.

## ✅ Already Deployed
Your emergency response team has prepared:
• 🧠 Knowledge Base (20 legal documents processed & indexed)
• 🤖 Bedrock Agent (connected to Knowledge Base for intelligent queries)
• 🖥️ EC2 Instance (pre-configured with Python & security groups)
• 📶 Elastic IP (static public IP address assigned)
• 🔐 IAM Permissions (Bedrock Agent access & SSM connectivity enabled)
• 📱 Streamlit App Code (emergency legal discovery interface ready)

## 🔍 Understanding the Search Interface

What You're Deploying

A real-time web application that connects to your Bedrock Agent, allowing legal teams to ask questions like "What evidence shows MegaTech executives knew about battery defects?" and get instant AI-powered answers with citations from the Knowledge Base.

Key Components:

🖥️ Streamlit Frontend
Clean web interface for legal queries
🤖 Bedrock Agent Integration
Direct API connection to intelligent Agent with Knowledge Base access
⚡ Real-time Results
Instant semantic search with citations
🔒 Secure Access
Protected EC2 deployment with Elastic IP

## 🎯 Your Mission

Operation: Interface Lightning

1. Configure Security Group Access 🔗
Add both your public IP and the EC2's public IP to the security group ingress rules for port 8501
2. Access EC2 Instance 🖥
Connect to EC2 via Session Manager to prepare for deployment
3. Deploy Application 📦
Download app file, install dependencies, and launch Streamlit interface
4. Test Search System ⚡
Connect to the Streamlit website and verify real-time document queries work

## 🌐 Configure Security Group Access
Step 1 - Update Security Group:
1. Get your public IP: Visit https://whatismyipaddress.com
2. Go to EC2 Console → Security Groups → jam-streamlit-sg-{account-id}
3. Edit inbound rules → Add rule: TCP, Port 8501, Source: YOUR_PUBLIC_IP/32
4. IMPORTANT: Also add rule: TCP, Port 8501, Source: 0.0.0.0/0 (required for validation function, delete after passing task 2)

cd /tmp

**2. Download the app file**
wget https://aws-jam-challenge-resources.s3.amazonaws.com/legal_document_discovery/app.py
